“There will be volunteers,” the German replied with a smile.

Everyone looked around at the door again: it creaked, and the second princess, having prepared the drink prescribed by Lorrain, carried it to the sick man. The German doctor approached Lorrain.

“Could he perhaps last until tomorrow morning?” asked the German, pronouncing the French badly.

Lorrain pursed his lips and sternly wagged a finger from side to side before his nose.

“Tonight, no later,” he said quietly, with a decorous smile of self-satisfaction at his ability to understand and express the sick man’s condition clearly, and walked away.

————

Meanwhile, Prince Vasili opened the door to the princess’s room.

The room was dimly lit; only two icon lamps burned before the icons, and there was a pleasant smell of incense and flowers. The whole room was crowded with small pieces of furniture: chiffoniers, little cupboards, and tables. The white covers of a tall feather bed could be seen beyond the screens. A little dog barked.

“Ah, is that you, my cousin?”

She rose and smoothed her hair, which was always, even now, so extraordinarily sleek that it looked as though it had been made in one piece with her head and coated with varnish.

“What is it? Has something happened?” she asked. “I was already so frightened.”

“Nothing, everything is the same; I have only come to talk to you, Catiche, about a matter,” said the prince, wearily sitting down in the armchair from which she had risen. “How hot you have made it in here, though,” he said. “Well, sit down here; let us talk.”

“I thought something might have happened,” said the princess, and with her unchanging, stonily severe expression she sat down opposite the prince, preparing to listen.

“I wanted to fall asleep, my cousin, but I cannot.”

“Well, then, my dear?” said Prince Vasili, taking the princess’s hand and, as was his habit, bending it downward.

It was evident that this “Well, then” referred to many things which, without naming them, they both understood.

The princess, with her dry, straight torso disproportionately long in relation to her legs, looked directly and impassively at the prince with her protuberant gray eyes. She shook her head and, sighing, looked at the icons. Her gesture could have been interpreted both as an expression of sorrow and devotion and as an expression of weariness and hope for a speedy rest. Prince Vasili interpreted it as an expression of weariness.

“And as for me,” he said, “do you think it is any easier? I am worn out like a post horse; but all the same, I must talk to you, Catiche, and very seriously.”

Prince Vasili fell silent, and his cheeks began twitching nervously, first on one side and then on the other, giving his face an unpleasant expression that never appeared on Prince Vasili’s face when he was in drawing rooms. His eyes, too, were not as they usually were: at one moment they looked insolently jocular, and at the next they glanced around in fright.

The princess, holding the little dog on her lap with her dry, thin hands, looked attentively into Prince Vasili’s eyes; but it was evident that she would not break the silence with a question, even if she had to remain silent until morning.

“You see, my dear princess and cousin, Katerina Semyonovna,” Prince Vasili continued, evidently not without an inner struggle as he began to continue his speech, “at moments such as this, one must think of everything. One must think of the future, of all of you... I love you all as I do my own children; you know that.”

The princess continued to look at him just as dully and motionlessly.

“Finally, I must think of my own family as well,” Prince Vasili continued, angrily pushing the little table away from him and not looking at her. “You know, Catiche, that you three Mamontov sisters, and my wife as well, are the count’s only direct heirs. I know, I know how difficult it is for you to speak and think about such things. It is no easier for me; but, my friend, I am in my sixth decade and must be prepared for anything. Do you know that I sent for Pierre, and that the count, pointing directly at his portrait, demanded that he be brought to him?”

Prince Vasili looked questioningly at the princess, but could not tell whether she grasped what he had said to her or was merely looking at him...

“There is one thing I never cease imploring God for, my cousin,” she replied, “that He may have mercy on him and grant his beautiful soul a peaceful departure from this...”

“Yes, that is so,” Prince Vasili continued impatiently, rubbing his bald head and once again spitefully pulling toward him the table he had pushed away, “but finally... finally, the point is that you yourself know that last winter the count wrote a will by which he left the entire estate to Pierre, passing over the direct heirs and us.”

“He has written any number of wills!” the princess said calmly. “But he could not leave it to Pierre. Pierre is illegitimate.”

“My dear,” Prince Vasili suddenly said, pulling the table close against himself, becoming animated, and beginning to speak more rapidly, “but what if a letter has been written to the sovereign, and the count asks him to legitimize Pierre? You understand, in view of the count’s services, his request will be granted...”

The princess smiled as people smile when they think they know more about a matter than those with whom they are speaking.

“I shall tell you more,” Prince Vasili continued, seizing her hand. “The letter was written, though it was not sent, and the sovereign knew about it. The only question is whether it has been destroyed or not. If not, then as soon as it is all over”—Prince Vasili sighed, thereby making clear what he meant by the words “it is all over”—“and the count’s papers are opened, the will and the letter will be delivered to the sovereign, and his request will certainly be granted. Pierre, as his legitimate son, will receive everything.”

“And our share?” asked the princess, smiling ironically as though anything but that could happen.

“But, my poor Catiche, it is as clear as day. He will then be the sole legitimate heir to everything, and you will not receive even this. You must know, my dear, whether the will and the letter were written and whether they were destroyed. And if for some reason they have been forgotten, then you must know where they are and find them, because...”

“That is all that was lacking!” the princess interrupted him, smiling sardonically without changing the expression of her eyes. “I am a woman; in your opinion, we are all fools; but I know enough to know that an illegitimate son cannot inherit... A bastard,” she added, believing that with this translation she had conclusively shown the prince the groundlessness of his argument.

“How can you still fail to understand, Catiche! You are so clever; how can you fail to understand? If the count wrote a letter to the sovereign asking him to recognize his son as legitimate, then Pierre will no longer be Pierre, but Count Bezukhov, and then he will receive everything under the will. And if the will and the letter have not been destroyed, then nothing will remain to you except the consolation that you were virtuous and all that follows from it. That is certain.”

“Well, all right, all right, you can tell us afterward,” Princess Marya said, blushing.

“Allow me to ask her,” said Pierre. “Did you see it yourself?” he asked.

“Why, of course, father, I myself was vouchsafed the sight. There was such a radiance on the holy face, like the light of heaven, and from the little cheek of the Holy Mother it kept dripping and dripping...”

“But surely that is a fraud,” Pierre said ingenuously, listening attentively to the pilgrim woman.

“Oh, father, what are you saying!” Pelageyushka exclaimed in horror, turning to Princess Marya for protection.

“They are deceiving the people,” he repeated.

“Lord Jesus Christ,” said the pilgrim woman, crossing herself. “Oh, do not say that, father. There was one gen’ral who did not believe and said, ‘The monks are deceiving people,’ and no sooner had he said it than he went blind. And he dreamed that the Holy Mother of the Caves came to him and said, ‘Believe in me, and I shall heal you.’ So he began begging: take me to her, take me to her. I am telling you the true truth, I saw it myself. They brought him blind straight to her; he went up, fell down, and said, ‘Heal me! I’ll give you,’ he says, ‘what the Tsar bestowed upon me.’ I saw it myself, father: the star is set right into her. And what happened?—he regained his sight! It is a sin to speak that way. God will punish you,” she said, turning admonishingly to Pierre.

“But how did the star come to be in the icon?” asked Pierre.

“Was the Holy Mother promoted to general too?” Prince Andrei said with a smile.

Pelageyushka suddenly turned pale and threw up her hands.

“Father, father, it is a sin for you—you have a son!” she began, suddenly going from pallor to a vivid flush.

“Father, what a thing you have said; may God forgive you.” She crossed herself. “Lord, forgive him. Mistress, what is this?...” she said, turning to Princess Marya. She rose and, almost weeping, began gathering up her little bag. It was evident that she was both frightened and ashamed to be accepting benefactions in a house where such things could be said, and sorry that she must now forgo the benefactions of this house.

“Well, whatever has come over you?” said Princess Marya. “Why did you come to me?...”

“No, I was only joking, Pelageyushka,” said Pierre. “Princess, upon my word, I did not mean to offend her; I was only... Do not think anything of it; I was joking,” he said, smiling timidly and wishing to make amends for his fault.

Pelageyushka paused distrustfully, but there was such sincere remorse in Pierre’s face, and Prince Andrei looked so gently first at Pelageyushka and then at Pierre, that she gradually calmed down.

XIV

The pilgrim woman calmed down and, once more drawn into conversation, went on for a long time telling them about Father Amphilokhy, who led such a holy life that his little hand smelled of incense, and about how some monks she knew, on her latest pilgrimage to Kiev, had given her the keys to the caves, and how, taking some dry rusks with her, she had spent two days in the caves with the saints. “I pray to one, read the prayers, then go to another. I take a nap, then go and venerate the relics again; and there is such stillness there, mistress, such grace, that one does not even want to come back out into God’s daylight.”

Pierre listened to her attentively and seriously. Prince Andrei left the room. Following him, and leaving God’s people to finish their tea, Princess Marya led Pierre into the drawing room.

“You are very kind,” she said to him.

“Oh, I truly did not mean to offend her; I understand and esteem those feelings so highly.”

Princess Marya looked at him in silence and smiled tenderly.

“I have known you for a long time, you know, and I love you as a brother,” she said. “How did you find Andrei?” she asked hurriedly, giving him no time to say anything in reply to her affectionate words. “He worries me greatly. His health is better in winter, but last spring the wound opened, and the doctor said he ought to go away for treatment. And I am very much afraid for him morally. He does not have a nature like ours, like women’s, to suffer through his grief and weep it out. He carries it within himself. Today he is cheerful and animated, but it is your arrival that has had such an effect on him; he is rarely like this. If only you could persuade him to go abroad! He needs activity, and this even, quiet life is destroying him. Others do not notice, but I see it.”

Toward ten o’clock the footmen rushed to the front steps when they heard the bells of the old prince’s approaching carriage. Prince Andrei and Pierre also went out onto the steps.

“Who is this?” asked the old prince as he got out of the carriage and saw Pierre.

“Ah! Very glad! Kiss me,” he said, recognizing who the unfamiliar young man was.

The old prince was in good spirits and made much of Pierre.

Before supper, Prince Andrei, on returning to his father’s study, found the old prince engaged in a heated argument with Pierre. Pierre was maintaining that a time would come when there would be no more war. The old prince disputed him, teasing but without anger.

“Drain the blood from people’s veins and pour in water, and then there will be no war. Women’s drivel, women’s drivel,” he said, but nevertheless patted Pierre affectionately on the shoulder and went over to the table where Prince Andrei, evidently not wishing to join the conversation, was sorting through papers the prince had brought from town. The old prince went up to him and began talking about business.

“The marshal, Count Rostov, failed to furnish half the men. He came to town and took it into his head to invite me to dinner—I gave him a dinner he won’t forget... But look this over... Well, brother,” Prince Nikolai Andreich said, turning to his son and slapping Pierre on the shoulder, “that friend of yours is a fine fellow; I have grown fond of him! He fires me up. Another man may say clever things, but I have no wish to listen; while he talks nonsense and still fires me up, an old man. Well, go, go,” he said. “Perhaps I’ll come and sit with you at supper. We’ll argue again. Love that fool of mine, Princess Marya,” he shouted to Pierre from the doorway.

Only now, on this visit to Bald Hills, did Pierre appreciate the full strength and charm of his friendship with Prince Andrei. This charm manifested itself not so much in his relations with Andrei himself as in his relations with all Andrei’s relatives and household. With the old, stern prince and the gentle and timid Princess Marya, although he scarcely knew them, Pierre immediately felt like an old friend. They all already loved him. It was not only Princess Marya, won over by his gentle treatment of the pilgrim women, who looked at him with the most radiant expression; little Prince Nikolai, a year old, as his grandfather called him, smiled at Pierre and went into his arms. Mikhail Ivanych and Mademoiselle Bourienne looked at him with delighted smiles when he spoke with the old prince.

The old prince came out to supper: it was obvious to Pierre that he had done so for his sake. During both days of Pierre’s stay at Bald Hills, he was extraordinarily affectionate toward him and told him to come and visit again.

When Pierre had left and all the members of the family gathered together, they began passing judgment on him, as always happens after the departure of a new person; and, as rarely happens, they all said nothing but good things about him.

Two hours after this, Prince Andrei entered his father’s study with quiet steps. The old man already knew everything. He was standing right by the door, and as soon as it opened, the old man silently clasped his son’s neck with his aged, hard hands, like a vise, and sobbed like a child.

Three days later the funeral service was held for the little princess, and, taking leave of her, Prince Andrei mounted the steps to the coffin. And in the coffin was the same face, though with closed eyes. “Ah, what have you done to me?” it kept saying, and Prince Andrei felt that something had been torn away in his soul, that he was guilty of a wrong he could neither make amends for nor forget. He could not weep. The old man also went up and kissed her waxen little hand, which lay calmly and loftily upon the other, and to him her face said: “Ah, what have you done to me, and why?” And the old man turned away angrily when he saw that face.

Five days later, the young Prince Nikolai Andreich was baptized. The nurse held the swaddling clothes in place with her chin while the priest, with a goose feather, anointed the boy’s wrinkled red little palms and soles.

The godfather—the grandfather—afraid of dropping him and trembling, carried the infant around the dented tin font and handed him to the godmother, Princess Marya. Prince Andrei, faint with fear lest they drown the child, sat in another room awaiting the end of the sacrament. He looked joyfully at the child when the nurse brought him out to him, and nodded approvingly when the nurse informed him that the little piece of wax with hairs on it, which had been thrown into the font, had not sunk but had floated upon the water.

X.

Rostov’s involvement in Dolokhov’s duel with Bezukhov was hushed up through the efforts of the old count, and instead of being reduced to the ranks, as he had expected, Rostov was appointed an aide-de-camp to the governor-general of Moscow. Consequently, he could not go to the country with the whole family, but remained at his new post in Moscow throughout the summer. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov became especially close to him during the period of his recovery. Dolokhov lay ill at the home of his mother, who loved him passionately and tenderly. The old lady, Marya Ivanovna, who had grown fond of Rostov because of his friendship with Fedya, often spoke to him about her son.

“Yes, Count, he is too noble and pure in soul,” she would say, “for our present, corrupt world. No one loves virtue; it is an eyesore to everyone. Now tell me, Count, was that fair, was that honorable on Bezukhov’s part? And Fedya, in his nobility, loved him, and even now never says anything bad about him. In Petersburg, those escapades with the district police superintendent—they were playing some prank there, weren’t they, and they did it together? Yet nothing happened to Bezukhov, while Fedya bore the whole burden on his shoulders! And what he endured! Granted, they reinstated him, but how could they not reinstate him? I should think there were not many brave men and sons of the fatherland like him there. And now—this duel? Have those people any sense of honor? Knowing that he is an only son, to challenge him to a duel and shoot so straight! It is a good thing God had mercy on us. And what for? Well, who in our time does not have an affair? What of it, if he is so jealous? I understand—he could have made him feel it before, but it had gone on for a whole year. And then what does he do but challenge him to a duel, assuming that Fedya would not fight because he owed him money. What baseness! What vileness! I know that you understood Fedya, my dear Count; that is why I love you with all my soul, believe me. Few people understand him. His is such a lofty, heavenly soul!”

During his recovery, Dolokhov himself often said things to Rostov that no one could possibly have expected from him.

“They consider me a wicked man, I know,” he said, “and let them. I want to know no one except those whom I love; but whomever I love, I love so much that I would give my life for him, while all the rest I will crush if they stand in my way. I have an adored, inestimable mother, two or three friends, including you, and I pay attention to the rest only insofar as they are useful or harmful. And almost all of them are harmful, especially women. Yes, my dear,” he continued, “I have met loving, noble, exalted men; but women—apart from venal creatures, countesses or kitchen maids, it makes no difference—I have not yet met. I have not yet encountered that heavenly purity and devotion which I seek in a woman. If I found such a woman, I would give my life for her. But these!” He made a contemptuous gesture. “And will you believe me, if I still value life, I value it only because I still hope to meet such a heavenly being, one who would regenerate, purify, and exalt me. But you do not understand this.”

“No, I understand very well,” replied Rostov, who was under the influence of his new friend.

—————

In the autumn, the Rostov family returned to Moscow. At the beginning of winter, Denisov returned as well and stayed with the Rostovs. This first part of the winter of 1806, which Nikolai Rostov spent in Moscow, was one of the happiest and merriest times for him and for his whole family. Nikolai brought many young men with him to his parents’ house. Vera was a beautiful young woman of twenty; Sonya was a sixteen-year-old girl in all the loveliness of a flower that had only just opened; Natasha was half young lady, half child, now childishly amusing, now girlishly enchanting.

At that time a certain special atmosphere of amorousness arose in the Rostovs’ house, as happens in a house where there are very charming and very young girls. Every young man who came to the Rostovs’ house, looking at those young, impressionable, maidenly faces smiling at something—probably at their own happiness—at all that lively running to and fro, listening to the disjointed yet affectionate prattle of the young women, friendly to everyone, ready for anything, and full of hope, listening to those disjointed sounds, now of singing, now of music, experienced the same feeling of readiness for love and expectation of happiness that the young people of the Rostov household themselves experienced.

Among the young men introduced by Rostov, one of the foremost was Dolokhov, who pleased everyone in the house except Natasha. She nearly quarreled with her brother over Dolokhov. She insisted that he was a wicked man, that in the duel with Bezukhov, Pierre had been in the right and Dolokhov in the wrong, and that Dolokhov was unpleasant and unnatural.

“There is nothing for me to understand!” Natasha cried with stubborn willfulness. “He is wicked and has no feelings. Why, I love your Denisov; he is a carouser and everything, but I love him all the same, so that means I do understand. I don’t know how to explain it to you; everything about him is calculated, and I don’t like that. But Denisov...”

“Well, Denisov is another matter,” Nikolai replied, making it clear that, compared with Dolokhov, even Denisov was nothing. “You have to understand what kind of soul this Dolokhov has; you have to see him with his mother. What a heart!”

During the last period of her stay in Voronezh, Princess Marya experienced the greatest happiness of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or agitated her. This love filled her whole soul, had become an inseparable part of her very self, and she no longer struggled against it. Lately Princess Marya had become convinced—although she had never clearly and explicitly put it into words to herself—convinced that she was loved and that she loved. She became convinced of this at her last meeting with Nikolai, when he came to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Nikolai did not hint by a single word that now (if Prince Andrei recovered) the former relations between him and Natasha might be renewed, but Princess Marya saw from his face that he knew and thought this. And, despite that, his manner toward her—careful, tender, and loving—not only did not change, but he seemed to rejoice that the kinship now existing between him and Princess Marya allowed him to express more freely to her his friendship-love, as Princess Marya sometimes thought of it. Princess Marya knew that she loved for the first and last time in her life, and felt that she was loved, and was happy and at peace in that respect.

But this happiness of one side of her soul not only did not prevent her from feeling in all its force her grief over her brother; on the contrary, this peace of mind in one respect gave her a greater capacity to surrender herself wholly to her feeling for her brother. This feeling was so strong in the first moments after her departure from Voronezh that those seeing her off, looking at her tormented, despairing face, were certain that she would inevitably fall ill on the way; but it was precisely the difficulties and cares of the journey, which Princess Marya took up with such energy, that saved her for a time from her grief and gave her strength.

As always happens during a journey, Princess Marya thought only about the journey itself, forgetting what its purpose was. But as they approached Yaroslavl, when what might await her revealed itself again—and not many days hence, but that very evening—Princess Marya’s agitation reached its utmost limits.

When the haiduk who had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and what condition Prince Andrei was in met the large arriving carriage at the town gate, he was horrified when he saw the princess’s terribly pale face thrust out toward him from the window.

“I found out everything, Your Serene Highness: the Rostovs are staying on the square, in the house of the merchant Bronnikov. Not far away, right above the Volga,” said the haiduk.

Princess Marya looked into his face in frightened inquiry, not understanding why he did not answer the main question: what about her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked the question for the princess.

“What about the prince?” she asked.

“His Serene Highness is staying with them in the same house.”

“So he is alive,” thought the princess, and quietly asked, “How is he?”

“The servants say he is still in the same condition.”

The princess did not ask what “still in the same condition” meant, and, merely casting a brief, unnoticed glance at seven-year-old Nikolushka, who sat before her rejoicing at the sight of the town, lowered her head and did not raise it until the heavy carriage, rumbling, jolting, and swaying, stopped somewhere. The folding steps clattered as they were let down.

The doors opened. To the left was water—a broad river; to the right, a porch; on the porch were people, servants, and a certain rosy-cheeked girl with a thick black braid, who smiled with unpleasant insincerity, as it seemed to Princess Marya (this was Sonya). The princess ran up the steps; the girl with the feigned smile said, “This way, this way!” and the princess found herself in the anteroom before an old woman with Oriental features, who came quickly toward her with a deeply moved expression. This was the old countess. She embraced Princess Marya and began kissing her.

“My child!” she said. “I love you and have known you for a long time.”

Despite all her agitation, Princess Marya understood that this was the countess and that she had to say something to her. Without herself knowing how, she uttered some courteous words in French, in the same tone as those that had been spoken to her, and asked, “How is he?”

“The doctor says there is no danger,” said the countess, but as she said this, she raised her eyes with a sigh, and in that gesture was an expression that contradicted her words.

“Where is he? May I see him, may I?” asked the princess.

“In a moment, Princess, in a moment, my dear. Is this his son?” she said, turning to Nikolushka, who was coming in with Desalles. “There will be room for all of us; the house is large. Oh, what a charming boy!”

The countess led the princess into the drawing room. Sonya was talking with Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy. The old count entered the room, greeting the princess. The old count had changed enormously since the princess had last seen him. Then he had been a lively, cheerful, self-assured old man; now he seemed a pitiful, lost man. As he spoke with the princess, he kept looking around, as though asking everyone whether he was doing what he ought to do. After the destruction of Moscow and of his estate, knocked out of his accustomed rut, he had evidently lost his sense of his own significance and felt that there was no longer any place for him in life.

Despite her one desire to see her brother as soon as possible, and despite her vexation that at this moment, when all she wanted was to see him, they were occupying her and insincerely praising her nephew, the princess noticed everything that was happening around her and felt the necessity of submitting for a time to this new order into which she had entered. She knew that all this was necessary, and although it was difficult for her, she was not vexed with them.

“This is my niece,” said the count, presenting Sonya. “You do not know her, Princess?”

The princess turned to her and, trying to stifle the hostile feeling toward this girl that had arisen in her soul, kissed her. But she found it oppressive that the state of mind of everyone around her was so far removed from what was in her own soul.

“Where is he?” she asked once more, addressing everyone.

“He is downstairs; Natasha is with him,” Sonya answered, blushing. “We have sent to find out. I think you must be tired, Princess?”

Tears of vexation came into the princess’s eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to get to him when light, rapid, seemingly cheerful footsteps were heard at the door. The princess looked around and saw Natasha almost running in—that Natasha whom she had disliked so much at their long-ago meeting in Moscow.

But before the princess had time to look at this Natasha’s face, she understood that this was her sincere companion in grief, and therefore her friend. She rushed to meet her and, embracing her, began to weep on her shoulder.

As soon as Natasha, who had been sitting at Prince Andrei’s bedside, learned of Princess Marya’s arrival, she quietly left his room with those rapid, seemingly cheerful footsteps, as they had appeared to Princess Marya, and ran to her.

On her agitated face, when she ran into the room, there was only one expression—the expression of love, of boundless love for him, for her, for everything that was close to the man she loved; an expression of pity, of suffering for others, and of a passionate desire to give all of herself in order to help them. It was evident that at that moment there was not a single thought in Natasha’s soul about herself or about her relations with him.

Pierre smiled, but from his smile it was evident that he understood that it was not the anecdote about Sergei Kuzmich that interested Prince Vasili at that moment; and Prince Vasili understood that Pierre understood this. Prince Vasili suddenly muttered something and went out. It seemed to Pierre that even Prince Vasili was embarrassed. The sight of this old man of the world’s embarrassment touched Pierre; he looked back at Hélène—and she, it seemed, was embarrassed and said with her look, “Well, it is your own fault.”

“I must inevitably cross the threshold, but I cannot, I cannot,” thought Pierre, and once again began talking about something extraneous, about Sergei Kuzmich, asking what the anecdote was, since he had not heard it. Hélène replied with a smile that she did not know either.

When Prince Vasili entered the drawing room, the princess was speaking quietly to an elderly lady about Pierre.

“Of course, it is a very brilliant match, but happiness, my dear...”

“Marriages are made in heaven,” replied the elderly lady.

Prince Vasili, as though not listening to the ladies, walked to a far corner and sat down on a sofa. He closed his eyes and seemed to doze. His head had begun to droop, and he woke up.

“Aline,” he said to his wife, “go and see what they are doing.”

The princess approached the door, walked past it with a significant, indifferent air, and looked into the drawing room. Pierre and Hélène were still sitting and talking in the same way.

“Still the same,” she replied to her husband.

Prince Vasili frowned and twisted his mouth to one side; his cheeks began to twitch with the unpleasant, coarse expression peculiar to him. Shaking himself, he rose, threw back his head, and, with resolute steps, passed the ladies and went into the small drawing room. With quick steps he approached Pierre joyfully. The prince’s face was so extraordinarily solemn that Pierre rose in alarm when he saw him.

“Thank God!” he said. “My wife has told me everything!” He embraced Pierre with one arm and his daughter with the other. “My dear Lelya! I am very, very glad.” His voice trembled. “I loved your father... and she will be a good wife to you... May God bless you!”

He embraced his daughter, then Pierre again, and kissed him with his old man’s mouth. Tears actually moistened his cheeks.

“Princess, come here,” he shouted.

The princess came out and began to weep too. The elderly lady was also wiping her eyes with her handkerchief. Pierre was kissed, and several times he kissed the hand of the beautiful Hélène. After a while they were left alone again.

“All this was bound to happen and could not have happened otherwise,” thought Pierre, “so there is no point in asking whether it is good or bad. It is good because it is settled, and the former agonizing doubt is gone.” Pierre silently held his fiancée’s hand and looked at her beautiful bosom as it rose and fell.

“Hélène!” he said aloud, and stopped.

“Something special is said on these occasions,” he thought, but he could not for the life of him remember exactly what was said on these occasions. He looked into her face. She moved closer to him. Her face flushed.

“Oh, take off those... what are they...” She pointed at his spectacles.

Pierre took off his spectacles, and his eyes, in addition to the general strangeness of the eyes of people who have removed their spectacles, looked frightened and questioning. He wanted to bend over her hand and kiss it; but with a swift and rough movement of her head she intercepted his lips and brought them together with her own. Her face struck Pierre by its changed, unpleasantly bewildered expression.

“Now it is too late, it is all over; and besides, I love her,” thought Pierre.

“I love you!” he said, remembering what had to be said on these occasions; but the words sounded so feeble that he felt ashamed of himself.

A month and a half later he was married in church and took up residence, as people said, the happy possessor of a beautiful wife and millions, in the large, newly refurbished St. Petersburg house of the Counts Bezukhov.

III.

In December 1805, old Prince Nikolai Andreich Bolkonsky received a letter from Prince Vasili informing him of his arrival together with his son. (“I am traveling on an inspection, and of course a detour of sixty miles is nothing to me in order to visit you, my most esteemed benefactor,” he wrote, “and my Anatole is accompanying me and is going to the army; and I hope that you will permit him personally to express to you the profound respect which, in imitation of his father, he bears for you.”)

“So there is no need even to take Marie out into society: the suitors come to us themselves,” the little princess said incautiously when she heard about it.

Prince Nikolai Andreich grimaced and said nothing.

Two weeks after the letter was received, Prince Vasili’s servants arrived ahead of him one evening, and the next day he himself arrived with his son.

Old Bolkonsky had always had a low opinion of Prince Vasili’s character, and all the more so in recent years, when Prince Vasili had risen far in rank and honors during the new reigns of Paul and Alexander. Now, from the hints in the letter and from the little princess, he understood what the matter was, and his low opinion of Prince Vasili turned in Prince Nikolai Andreich’s soul into a feeling of hostile contempt. He constantly snorted when speaking of him. On the day Prince Vasili was to arrive, Prince Nikolai Andreich was especially displeased and out of humor. Whether he was out of humor because Prince Vasili was coming, or especially displeased by Prince Vasili’s arrival because he was out of humor, he was out of humor; and that very morning Tikhon had advised the architect against going in to make his report to the prince.

“Do you hear how he is walking?” said Tikhon, drawing the architect’s attention to the sound of the prince’s footsteps. “He comes down on the whole heel—we know what that means...”

Nevertheless, as usual, during the ninth hour the prince went out for his walk in his velvet fur coat with a sable collar and a matching cap. Snow had fallen the day before. The path along which Prince Nikolai Andreich used to walk to the conservatory had been cleared, the marks of the broom were visible in the scattered snow, and a shovel had been thrust into the loose bank of snow running along both sides of the path. The prince walked through the conservatories, the servants’ quarters, and the outbuildings, frowning and silent.

“Can a sleigh get through?” he asked the steward, a dignified man who resembled his master in face and manner and had accompanied him back to the house.

“The snow is deep, Your Excellency. I have already ordered them to clear it along the avenue.”

The prince bowed his head and approached the front steps. “Glory be to You, O Lord,” thought the steward, “the storm cloud has passed!”

“It was difficult to get through, Your Excellency,” the steward added. “We heard, Your Excellency, that a minister would be pleased to call upon Your Excellency?”

The prince turned to the steward and fixed him with frowning eyes.

“What? A minister? What minister? Who gave the order?” he began in his piercing, harsh voice. “They did not clear it for the princess, my daughter, but they did for a minister! I have no ministers!”

Nikolai, as always, having worn out two pairs of horses and still not managed to visit all the places where he needed to be and to which he had been invited, arrived home just before dinner. As soon as he entered, he noticed and felt the tension of the amorous atmosphere in the house, but in addition he noticed the strange confusion prevailing among some members of the company. Sonya, Dolokhov, the old countess, and, to some extent, Natasha were particularly agitated. Nikolai realized that something must have happened before dinner between Sonya and Dolokhov and, with his characteristic sensitivity of heart, was very tender and cautious in his dealings with them both during dinner. That same evening, the third day of the holidays, there was to be one of those balls at Iogel’s—the dancing master’s—which he gave during the holidays for all his male and female pupils.

“Nikolenka, are you going to Iogel’s? Please go,” Natasha said to him. “He asked especially for you, and Vasily Dmitrich”—this was Denisov—“is going.”

“Where would I not go at the countess’s command!” said Denisov, who had jokingly placed himself in the Rostovs’ household on the footing of Natasha’s knight. “I am ready to dance the shawl dance.”

“If I have time! I promised the Arkharovs; they are having an evening,” said Nikolai.

“And you?…” he said, turning to Dolokhov. And no sooner had he asked than he realized that he should not have asked it.

“Yes, perhaps…” Dolokhov replied coldly and angrily, glancing at Sonya and then, frowning, looking again at Nikolai with exactly the same look with which he had regarded Pierre at the dinner at the club.

“There is something going on,” thought Nikolai, and he was still further confirmed in this supposition by the fact that Dolokhov left immediately after dinner. He called Natasha out and asked what it was.

“I was looking for you,” Natasha said, running out to him. “I told you, but you would never believe me,” she said triumphantly. “He proposed to Sonya.”

Little as Nikolai had concerned himself with Sonya during that time, something seemed to tear loose inside him when he heard this. Dolokhov was a respectable and, in some respects, brilliant match for Sonya, a penniless orphan. From the point of view of the old countess and society, she could not refuse him. And so Nikolai’s first feeling when he heard this was anger with Sonya. He was preparing to say, “And an excellent thing too; of course she must forget childhood promises and accept the proposal,” but before he had time to say it…

“Can you imagine! She refused him, refused him outright!” Natasha began. “She said that she loves someone else,” she added after a short silence.

“My Sonya could not have acted otherwise!” thought Nikolai.

“No matter how much Mama begged her, she refused, and I know she will not change her mind once she has said something…”

“And Mama begged her!” Nikolai said reproachfully.

“Yes,” said Natasha. “You know, Nikolenka, do not be angry; but I know that you will not marry her. I know—God knows why—but I know for certain that you will not marry her.”

“Well, you cannot possibly know that,” said Nikolai. “But I must talk to her. What a treasure that Sonya is!” he added with a smile.

“She is such a treasure! I shall send her to you.” And Natasha kissed her brother and ran away.

A minute later Sonya came in, frightened, confused, and guilty. Nikolai went up to her and kissed her hand. This was the first time during this visit that they had spoken face to face and about their love.

“Sophie,” he said, timidly at first and then more and more boldly, “if you wish to refuse not merely a brilliant and advantageous match; but he is a splendid, noble man… he is my friend…”

Sonya interrupted him.

“I have already refused him,” she said hurriedly.

“If you are refusing him for my sake, then I am afraid that I…”

Sonya interrupted him again. She looked at him with a pleading, frightened gaze.

“Nicolas, do not say this to me,” she said.

“No, I must. Perhaps it is presumption on my part, but it is better to say it. If you refuse him for my sake, then I must tell you the whole truth. I love you, I think, more than anyone…”

“That is enough for me,” Sonya said, flushing.

“No, but I have fallen in love a thousand times and shall fall in love again, although I have no such feeling of friendship, trust, and love for anyone as I have for you. Besides, I am young. Maman does not want it. Well, quite simply, I promise nothing. And I ask you to think about Dolokhov’s proposal,” he said, pronouncing his friend’s surname with difficulty.

“Do not say that to me. I want nothing. I love you as a brother, and I shall always love you, and I need nothing more.”

“You are an angel; I am not worthy of you, but I am only afraid of deceiving you.” Nikolai kissed her hand once more.

XII.

Iogel’s balls were the merriest in Moscow. So the mothers said as they watched their adolescent daughters performing the steps they had only just learned; so said the adolescent girls and boys themselves, who danced until they dropped; so said the grown young ladies and young men who came to these balls intending to condescend to them, only to find the very best entertainment there. That very year, two marriages resulted from these balls. Two pretty Princesses Gorchakov found bridegrooms and married, thereby adding still further to the fame of the balls. What was special about these balls was that there was no host or hostess: there was the good-natured Iogel, flitting about like thistledown and making bows according to all the rules of his art, who accepted lesson tickets from all his guests; and also that only those who wanted to dance and enjoy themselves as thirteen- and fourteen-year-old girls do when they put on long dresses for the first time still attended these balls. With rare exceptions, everyone was, or seemed, pretty: so rapturously did they all smile and so brightly did their little eyes glow. Sometimes the best female pupils even danced the shawl dance, and the best of them was Natasha, who was distinguished by her gracefulness; but at this, the last ball, they danced only écossaises, anglaises, and the mazurka, which had only just begun to come into fashion. Iogel had hired a ballroom in Bezukhov’s house, and the ball was a great success, as everyone said. There were many pretty girls, and the young Rostov ladies were among the prettiest. Both of them were particularly happy and merry. That evening Sonya, proud of Dolokhov’s proposal, of her refusal, and of her explanation with Nikolai, had been whirling about even at home, not letting the maid finish plaiting her hair, and now she shone through and through with impetuous joy.

Natasha, no less proud that for the first time she was wearing a long dress at a real ball, was even happier. They were both wearing white muslin dresses with pink ribbons.

Natasha fell in love from the very moment she entered the ball. She was not in love with anyone in particular, but she was in love with everyone. Whoever she happened to be looking at at any given moment, she was in love with that person.

“Oh, how wonderful!” she kept saying as she ran up to Sonya.

Nikolai and Denisov walked through the rooms, looking affectionately and protectively at the dancers.

“How sweet she is; she will be a beauty,” said Denisov.

“Who?”

“Countess Natasha,” Denisov replied.

“And how she dances—what grace!” he said again after a short silence.

“Who are you talking about?”

“Your sister,” Denisov shouted angrily.

Rostov smiled.

“My dear Count, you are one of my best pupils; you must dance,” little Iogel said as he approached Nikolai. “See how many pretty young ladies there are.” He addressed the same request to Denisov, who had also formerly been his pupil.

Anna Pavlovna smiled and promised to take Pierre in hand; she knew that he was related on his father’s side to Prince Vassily.

The elderly lady who had previously been sitting with my aunt rose hurriedly and caught up with Prince Vassily in the anteroom. All the earlier pretense of interest vanished from her face. Her kind, tear-worn face expressed only anxiety and fear.

“What, then, can you tell me, Prince, about my Boris?” she said, catching up with him in the anteroom. (She pronounced the name Boris with particular emphasis on the o.) “I cannot remain in Petersburg any longer. Tell me, what news can I take back to my poor boy?”

Although Prince Vassily listened to the elderly lady reluctantly and almost discourteously, and even showed impatience, she smiled at him tenderly and touchingly and, to prevent him from leaving, took him by the arm.

“What would it cost you to say one word to the sovereign, and he would be transferred straight into the Guards,” she pleaded.

“Believe me, I shall do everything I can, Princess,” Prince Vassily replied, “but it is difficult for me to ask the sovereign; I would advise you to approach Rumyantsev through Prince Golitsyn: that would be wiser.”

The elderly lady bore the name of Princess Drubetskaya, one of the finest families in Russia, but she was poor, had long since withdrawn from society, and had lost her former connections. She had now come to secure an appointment in the Guards for her only son. It was solely in order to see Prince Vassily that she had had herself announced and come to Anna Pavlovna’s soirée; it was solely for that reason that she had listened to the viscount’s story. Prince Vassily’s words frightened her; her once beautiful face expressed bitterness, but this lasted only a minute. She smiled again and clutched Prince Vassily’s arm more tightly.

“Listen, Prince,” she said, “I have never asked you for anything, I shall never ask you again, I have never reminded you of my father’s friendship with you. But now, I implore you in God’s name, do this for my son, and I shall regard you as my benefactor,” she added hurriedly. “No, do not be angry; promise me. I asked Golitsyn; he refused. Be the good boy you used to be,” she said, trying to smile while there were tears in her eyes.

“Papa, we shall be late,” said Princess Hélène, who was waiting by the door, turning her beautiful head upon her classically shaped shoulders.

But influence in society is capital that must be husbanded lest it disappear. Prince Vassily knew this, and, having once calculated that if he began asking favors for everyone who asked him, he would soon be unable to ask any for himself, he rarely made use of his influence. In Princess Drubetskaya’s case, however, after her renewed appeal, he felt something akin to a pang of conscience. She had reminded him of the truth: he owed his first steps in the service to her father. Moreover, he saw from her manner that she was one of those women, mothers especially, who, once they have taken something into their heads, will not desist until their wishes are fulfilled, and otherwise are prepared to pester one daily, every minute, and even to make scenes. This last consideration swayed him.

“My dear Anna Mikhailovna,” he said with his customary familiarity and boredom in his voice, “it is almost impossible for me to do what you want; but to prove to you how I love you and honor the memory of your late father, I shall do the impossible: your son will be transferred to the Guards; here is my hand on it. Are you satisfied?”

“My dear, you are my benefactor! I expected nothing else from you; I knew how kind you were.”

He was about to leave.

“Wait, two words. Once he has been transferred to the Guards...” She hesitated. “You are on good terms with Mikhail Ilarionovich Kutuzov; recommend Boris to him as an aide-de-camp. Then I would be at ease, and then...”

Prince Vassily smiled.

“I do not promise that. You do not know how Kutuzov has been besieged since he was appointed commander in chief. He himself told me that all the Moscow ladies had conspired to give him all their children as aides-de-camp.”

“No, promise me; I will not let you go, my dear benefactor.”

“Papa,” the beauty repeated again in the same tone, “we shall be late.”

“Well, au revoir, goodbye. You see?”

“So tomorrow you will report the matter to the sovereign?”

“Certainly, but I make no promise about Kutuzov.”

“No, promise, promise, Basile,” Anna Mikhailovna called after him, with the smile of a young coquette that must once have been characteristic of her but now suited her emaciated face so poorly.

She had evidently forgotten her age and, from habit, brought all the old feminine devices into play. But as soon as he had gone out, her face again assumed the same cold, feigned expression it had worn before. She returned to the circle in which the viscount was continuing his story and once again pretended to listen, waiting until it was time to leave, since her business had been accomplished.

“But what do you think of this latest comedy of the coronation at Milan?” said Anna Pavlovna. “And the new comedy of the peoples of Genoa and Lucca, who come to present their wishes to Monsieur Buonaparte. Monsieur Buonaparte seated on a throne and granting the wishes of nations! Adorable! No, it is enough to drive one mad! One would think the whole world had lost its head.”

Prince Andrei gave a slight smile, looking Anna Pavlovna straight in the face.

“‘God has given it to me; beware whoever touches it,’” he said (the words spoken by Bonaparte as the crown was placed upon his head). “They say he was very impressive when he pronounced those words,” he added, and once again repeated the words in Italian: “‘God has given it to me; woe to whoever touches it.’”

“I hope at last,” Anna Pavlovna continued, “that this was the drop of water that will make the glass overflow. The sovereigns can no longer endure this man, who threatens everything.”

“The sovereigns? I am not speaking of Russia,” said the viscount, courteously and hopelessly. “The sovereigns, madame! What have they done for Louis XVII, for the queen, for Madame Elisabeth? Nothing,” he continued, growing animated. “And believe me, they are suffering punishment for their betrayal of the Bourbon cause. The sovereigns? They send ambassadors to pay compliments to the usurper.”

And, sighing contemptuously, he changed his position again. Prince Hippolyte, who had long been looking at the viscount through his lorgnette, suddenly turned his whole body toward the little princess at these words and, after asking her for a needle, began showing her the Condé coat of arms by drawing it with the needle on the table. He explained the coat of arms to her with such an important air that one might have thought the princess had asked him to do so.

“Did you not receive my letter?” he asked, and, without waiting for an answer—which he would not have received in any case, because the princess could not speak—he went back and, together with the accoucheur, who entered behind him (he had met up with him at the last station), again went quickly up the stairs and again embraced his sister.

“What a fate!” he said. “Dear Masha!” And, taking off his fur coat and boots, he went to the little princess’s apartments.

IX.

The little princess lay on the pillows in a white cap. (The pains had only just released her.) Her black hair curled in strands about her inflamed, perspiring cheeks; her rosy, lovely little mouth, with its lip covered in dark down, was open, and she smiled joyfully. Prince Andrei entered the room and stopped before her, at the foot of the sofa on which she lay. Her shining eyes, gazing with childlike fear and agitation, came to rest on him without changing their expression. “I love you all; I have done no harm to anyone; why am I suffering? Help me,” her expression said. She saw her husband, but did not understand the significance of his appearing before her now. Prince Andrei walked around the sofa and kissed her on the forehead.

“My darling,” he said—a word he had never used to her. “God is merciful...” She looked at him questioningly, with childlike reproach.

“I expected help from you, and there is nothing, nothing—and you too!” said her eyes. She was not surprised that he had come; she did not understand that he had come. His arrival had no connection whatsoever with her sufferings or their relief. The torments began again, and Marya Bogdanovna advised Prince Andrei to leave the room.

The accoucheur entered the room. Prince Andrei went out and, meeting Princess Marya, approached her again. They began talking in whispers, but every moment their conversation fell silent. They waited and listened.

“Go, my friend,” said Princess Marya. Prince Andrei went back toward his wife and sat down in the adjoining room to wait. A woman came out of her room with a frightened face and became confused on seeing Prince Andrei. He covered his face with his hands and sat like that for several minutes. Piteous, helpless, animal-like moans could be heard from behind the door. Prince Andrei rose, went to the door, and tried to open it. Someone was holding the door shut.

“You cannot, you cannot!” a frightened voice said from within. He began pacing the room. The cries ceased; several more seconds passed. Suddenly a terrible scream—not her scream; she could not have screamed like that—rang out in the adjoining room. Prince Andrei rushed to the door; the scream ceased, and the cry of a child was heard.

“Why have they brought a child in there?” Prince Andrei thought in the first instant. “A child? What child?... Why is there a child in there? Or has a child been born?”

When he suddenly understood the full joyful significance of that cry, tears choked him, and, leaning with both hands on the windowsill, he began to sob and wept as children weep. The door opened. The doctor, his shirtsleeves rolled up, without his frock coat, pale and with a trembling jaw, came out of the room. Prince Andrei turned to him, but the doctor looked at him in bewilderment and, without saying a word, walked past. The woman ran out and, seeing Prince Andrei, faltered on the threshold. He entered his wife’s room. She lay dead in the same position in which he had seen her five minutes before, and the same expression, despite the sightless eyes and the pallor of her cheeks, remained on that lovely, childlike little face with its lip covered in dark down.

“I love you all and have done no harm to anyone, and what have you done to me?” said her lovely, pitiful, dead face. In a corner of the room, something small and red grunted and squeaked in Marya Bogdanovna’s trembling white hands.

Two hours after this, Prince Andrei entered his father’s study with quiet steps. The old man already knew everything. He was standing right by the door, and as soon as it opened, the old man silently clasped his son’s neck in his aged, hard hands, as though in a vise, and sobbed like a child.

Three days later the funeral service was held for the little princess, and, taking leave of her, Prince Andrei went up the steps to the coffin. And in the coffin was the same face, though its eyes were closed. “Ah, what have you done to me?” it still said, and Prince Andrei felt that something had been torn away in his soul, that he was guilty of a wrong he could neither set right nor forget. He could not weep. The old man also went up and kissed her waxen little hand, which lay calmly and loftily upon the other, and to him her face said: “Ah, what have you done to me, and why?” And the old man turned away angrily at the sight of that face.

Another five days later, the young prince Nikolai Andreitch was baptized. The nurse held the swaddling clothes in place with her chin while the priest, with a goose feather, anointed the boy’s wrinkled red little palms and feet.

The godfather-grandfather, trembling for fear of dropping him, carried the infant around the dented tin font and handed him to the godmother, Princess Marya. Prince Andrei, faint with fear that they might drown the child, sat in another room awaiting the end of the sacrament. He looked joyfully at the child when the nurse brought him out, and nodded his head approvingly when she told him that the bit of wax with the hairs, thrown into the font, had not sunk but had floated on the water.

X.

Rostov’s part in Dolokhov’s duel with Bezukhov was hushed up through the efforts of the old count, and instead of being reduced to the ranks, as he had expected, Rostov was appointed an aide-de-camp to the governor-general of Moscow. Consequently, he could not go to the country with the whole family, but remained at his new post in Moscow throughout the summer. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov became especially close to him during this period of his convalescence. Dolokhov lay ill at the home of his mother, who loved him passionately and tenderly. The old lady, Marya Ivanovna, who had grown fond of Rostov because of his friendship with Fedya, often spoke to him about her son.

“Yes, Count, he is too noble and pure of soul,” she would say, “for our present-day, corrupt world. No one loves virtue; it is an eyesore to everyone. Well, tell me, Count, was that fair, was that honorable of Bezukhov? And Fedya, in his nobility, loved him, and even now he never says anything bad about him. In Petersburg, those pranks with the district police officer—they were up to some joke or other there; why, they did it together, did they not? Yet Bezukhov suffered nothing, while Fedya bore the whole burden on his shoulders! And what he had to endure! Granted, they restored him to his rank, but how could they not restore it? I should think there were not many brave men and sons of the fatherland like him there. And now—this duel? Have those people any sense of honor? Knowing that he is an only son, to challenge him to a duel and shoot so straight! It is a good thing God had mercy on us. And what was it for? Well, who in our time does not have an affair? What of it, if he is so jealous? I understand; he could have made his feelings known earlier, but he let it go on for a whole year. And then what did he do? He challenged him to a duel, supposing Fedya would not fight because he owed him money. What baseness! What vileness! I know you understood Fedya, my dear Count; that is why I love you with all my soul, believe me. Few people understand him. His is such a lofty, heavenly soul!”

Marya Dmitrievna and the countess laughed, and all the guests followed their example. Everyone laughed not at Marya Dmitrievna’s reply, but at the inconceivable boldness and adroitness of this little girl, who knew how and dared to treat Marya Dmitrievna in such a way.

Natasha desisted only when she was told there would be pineapple ice cream. Champagne was served before the ice cream. The music began again, the count kissed the dear little countess, and the guests rose, congratulated the countess, and clinked glasses across the table with the count, the children, and one another. Once again the waiters began bustling about and the chairs clattered, and in the same order, but with redder faces, the guests returned to the drawing room and the count’s study.

XVII.

The Boston tables were opened out, parties were formed, and the count’s guests settled themselves in the two drawing rooms, the sofa room, and the library.

The count, holding his cards spread out in a fan, could barely keep himself from his habitual after-dinner nap and laughed at everything. The young people, urged on by the countess, gathered around the clavichord and the harp. Julie, at everyone’s request, was the first to play a little piece with variations on the harp, and then joined the other young ladies in asking Natasha and Nikolai, who were known for their musical gifts, to sing something. Natasha, who had been addressed as though she were grown up, was evidently very proud of this, but at the same time she was shy.

“What shall we sing?” she asked.

“The ‘Fountain,’” Nikolai replied.

“Well, let’s hurry, then. Boris, come here,” said Natasha. “But where is Sonya?”

She looked around and, seeing that her friend was not in the room, ran to find her.

Running into Sonya’s room and not finding her friend there, Natasha ran on to the nursery—and Sonya was not there either. Natasha realized that Sonya was in the corridor, on the trunk. The trunk in the corridor was the place of sorrows for the young female generation of the Rostov household. And indeed, Sonya, in her airy pink dress, crushing it beneath her, lay face down on the nurse’s dirty striped feather bed atop the trunk and, covering her face with her little fingers, sobbed convulsively, her bare little shoulders quivering. Natasha’s face, animated and festive all day for her name day, suddenly changed: her eyes became fixed, then her broad neck shuddered and the corners of her mouth drooped.

“Sonya! What is it?... What, what’s the matter with you? Oo-oo-oo!...”

And Natasha, opening her large mouth wide and becoming completely ugly, began bawling like a child, not knowing the reason and merely because Sonya was crying. Sonya tried to raise her head and tried to answer, but could not, and hid herself even more. Natasha wept, sitting down on the blue feather bed and embracing her friend. Summoning her strength, Sonya raised herself a little, began wiping away her tears, and told her what had happened.

“Nikolinka is leaving in a week; his... papers... have come through... he told me himself... But I still wouldn’t cry...”—she showed her a piece of paper she was holding in her hand: they were verses written by Nikolai—“I still wouldn’t cry, but you cannot... no one can understand... what a soul he has.”

And she began crying again because his soul was so good.

“It is all well for you... I am not jealous... I love you, and Boris too,” she said, having recovered her strength a little. “He is sweet... there are no obstacles for you. But Nikolai is my cousin... it would be necessary... the Metropolitan himself... and even then it is not allowed. And then, if Mamma...” (Sonya both regarded and called the countess her mother) “...she will say that I am ruining Nikolai’s career, that I have no heart, that I am ungrateful, but truly... by God...” She crossed herself. “I love her so much, and all of you too; only Vera... Why? What have I done to her? I am so grateful to you that I would gladly sacrifice everything, but I have nothing to sacrifice...”

Sonya could say no more and again hid her head in her hands and the feather bed. Natasha was beginning to calm down, but her face showed that she understood the full gravity of her friend’s sorrow.

“Sonya!” she said suddenly, as though she had guessed the true reason for her cousin’s distress. “Vera spoke to you after dinner, didn’t she? Yes?”

“Yes. Nikolai wrote these verses himself, and I copied out some others too; she found them on my table and said she would show them to Mamma, and she also said that I was ungrateful, that Mamma would never allow him to marry me, and that he would marry Julie. You see how he is with her all day long... Natasha! Why?...”

And once again she began to cry more bitterly than before. Natasha raised her up, embraced her, and, smiling through her tears, began to comfort her.

“Sonya, don’t believe her, darling, don’t believe her. Do you remember how the three of us talked with Nikolinka in the sofa room; remember, after supper? Why, we settled everything, how it would be. I no longer remember how, but remember how everything was so good and everything was possible. Why, Uncle Shinshin’s brother is married to his first cousin, and we are only third cousins. And Boris said it was quite possible. You know, I told him everything. And he is so clever and so good,” Natasha said. “Sonya, don’t cry, my precious darling, sweetheart, Sonya.” And she kissed her, laughing. “Vera is spiteful; never mind her! And everything will be all right, and she won’t tell Mamma; Nikolinka will tell her himself, and he has never even thought of Julie.”

And she kissed her on the head. Sonya raised herself, and the little kitten came to life, her little eyes sparkled, and she seemed ready at any moment to flick her tail, spring onto her soft paws, and begin playing with the ball of yarn again, as befitted her.

“Do you think so? Truly? By God?” she said, quickly straightening her dress and hair.

“Truly, by God!” Natasha replied, tucking back beneath her friend’s braid a stray lock of coarse hair.

And they both laughed.

“Well, let’s go and sing the ‘Fountain.’”

“Let’s go.”

“And do you know, that fat Pierre who was sitting opposite me is so funny!” Natasha said suddenly, stopping. “I am having such fun!”

And Natasha ran down the corridor.

Pierre was sitting in the drawing room, where Shinshin, treating him as someone newly arrived from abroad, had started a political conversation with him that Pierre found tedious and that others also joined. When the music began, Natasha entered the drawing room and, walking straight up to Pierre, said, laughing and blushing:

“Is that you, Clément?” he said. “Where the devil...” But he did not finish; recognizing his mistake and frowning slightly, he greeted Dolokhov as a stranger and asked how he could be of service. Dolokhov explained that he and his comrade were catching up with their regiment and, addressing everyone in general, asked whether the officers knew anything about the 6th Regiment. No one knew anything; and it seemed to Petya that the officers began looking him and Dolokhov over with hostility and suspicion. For several seconds everyone was silent.

“If you are counting on the evening soup, you have come too late,” said a voice from beyond the fire, with restrained laughter.

Dolokhov replied that they had eaten their fill and that they had to travel on that very night.

He handed the horses over to the soldier who was stirring the pot and squatted down by the fire beside the officer with the long neck. Without taking his eyes off Dolokhov, this officer looked at him and asked him once again what regiment he belonged to. Dolokhov did not answer, as though he had not heard the question, and, lighting a French pipe that he had taken from his pocket, asked the officers how safe the road ahead of them was from the Cossacks.

“The brigands are everywhere,” replied the officer beyond the fire.

Dolokhov said that the Cossacks were dangerous only to stragglers such as him and his comrade, but that the Cossacks probably did not dare attack large detachments, he added questioningly. No one answered.

“Well, now he will leave,” Petya thought every moment as he stood before the fire and listened to their conversation.

But Dolokhov again took up the conversation that had died away and began asking directly how many men they had in the battalion, how many battalions there were, and how many prisoners. Asking about the Russian prisoners who were with their detachment, Dolokhov said:

“It is a nasty business, dragging these corpses along behind one. It would be better to shoot this rabble,” and he laughed loudly with such a strange laugh that it seemed to Petya that the French would discover the deception at once, and he involuntarily stepped back from the fire. No one responded to Dolokhov’s words or laughter, and a French officer who could not be seen—he was lying wrapped in his greatcoat—raised himself and whispered something to his comrade. Dolokhov got up and called to the soldier with the horses.

“Will they bring the horses or not?” thought Petya, involuntarily moving closer to Dolokhov.

The horses were brought.

“Good day, gentlemen,” said Dolokhov.

Petya wanted to say “good evening” but could not finish the words. The officers were whispering something among themselves. Dolokhov took a long time mounting his horse, which would not stand still; then he rode out of the gate at a walk. Petya rode beside him, wanting to look back, yet not daring to, to see whether or not the French were running after them.

On reaching the road, Dolokhov did not ride back toward the fields, but along the village. At one point he stopped and listened.

“Do you hear?” he said.

Petya recognized the sound of Russian voices and saw the dark figures of Russian prisoners by the fires. Descending toward the bridge, Petya and Dolokhov rode past the sentry, who, without saying a word, paced gloomily over the bridge, and rode out into the hollow where the Cossacks were waiting.

“Well, goodbye now. Tell Denisov: at dawn, at the first shot,” said Dolokhov, and was about to ride off, but Petya caught hold of him with his hand.

“No!” he cried. “You are such a hero. Oh, how good! How splendid! How I love you.”

“All right, all right,” said Dolokhov, but Petya did not let go of him, and in the darkness Dolokhov made out that Petya was leaning toward him. He wanted to kiss him. Dolokhov kissed him, laughed, and, turning his horse, disappeared into the darkness.

X.

On returning to the guardhouse, Petya found Denisov in the entryway. Agitated, anxious, and vexed with himself for having let Petya go, Denisov had been awaiting him.

“Thank God!” he shouted. “Well, thank God!” he kept repeating as he listened to Petya’s enthusiastic account. “And damn you, I have not slept because of you!” Denisov said. “Well, thank God. Now lie down and sleep. We will still get a little nap before morning.”

“Yes... No,” said Petya. “I do not feel like sleeping yet. And I know myself: if I fall asleep, that will be the end of it. Besides, I am used to not sleeping before a battle.”

Petya sat in the hut for some time, joyfully recalling the details of his expedition and vividly imagining what would happen tomorrow. Then, noticing that Denisov had fallen asleep, he got up and went outside.

It was still completely dark outside. The rain had stopped, but drops were still falling from the trees. Near the guardhouse the black shapes of the Cossacks’ shelters and of horses tethered together could be seen. Behind the hut stood the dark shapes of two wagons with horses beside them, and in the ravine a dying fire glowed red. Not all the Cossacks and hussars were asleep: here and there, together with the sound of falling drops and the nearby sound of horses chewing, low voices could be heard, as though whispering.

Petya came out of the entryway, looked around in the darkness, and went over to the wagons. Someone was snoring beneath the wagons, and saddled horses stood around them, chewing oats. In the darkness Petya recognized his horse, which he called Karabakh, although it was a Little Russian horse, and went up to it.

“Well, Karabakh, tomorrow we shall do our duty,” he said, sniffing its nostrils and kissing it.

“What is it, sir, are you not sleeping?” said a Cossack sitting beneath a wagon.

“No; and... I believe your name is Likhachev? You see, I have only just come back. We went to the French.” And Petya gave the Cossack a detailed account not only of his expedition, but also of why he had gone and why he believed it was better to risk one’s life than to act at random and trust to luck.

“Well, you should have a little nap,” said the Cossack.

“No, I am used to it,” replied Petya. “And the flints in your pistols have not worn down, have they? I brought some with me. Do you need any? Take them.”

The Cossack leaned out from beneath the wagon to take a closer look at Petya.

“It is because I am used to doing everything properly,” said Petya. “Some people do things any old way and do not prepare, and then regret it afterward. I do not like that.”

“That is true,” said the Cossack.

“And here is another thing, please, my dear fellow: sharpen my saber for me; blunt it...” But Petya was afraid to tell a lie. “It has never been sharpened. Can it be done?”

“Why not? It can.”

Likhachev got up, rummaged through the packs, and Petya soon heard the martial sound of steel against a whetstone. He climbed onto the wagon and sat on its edge. Beneath the wagon, the Cossack was sharpening the saber.

“Well, are the fine fellows asleep?” said Petya.

“Some are asleep, and some are like this.”

“And what about the boy?”

“Vesenny? He has collapsed there in the entryway. He is sleeping from fright. He certainly was glad.”

For a long time after that Petya was silent, listening to the sounds. Footsteps were heard in the darkness, and a black figure appeared.

“What are you sharpening?” the man asked as he approached the wagon.

Berg was contented and happy. The smile of joy never left his face. The evening was very good and exactly like the other evenings he had seen. Everything was similar: the ladies’ refined conversations, the cards, the general at the card table raising his voice, the samovar, and the biscuits; but one thing was still lacking, something he had always seen at the evenings he wished to imitate. There was no loud conversation among the men, nor any argument about something important and intelligent. The general began such a conversation, and it was to this that Berg drew Pierre.

XXII.

The next day Prince Andrei went to dine with the Rostovs, having been invited by Count Ilya Andreich, and spent the entire day with them.

Everyone in the house knew for whom Prince Andrei had come, and, without concealing it, he tried all day to be with Natasha. Not only in Natasha’s soul—frightened, but happy and enraptured—but throughout the house, there was a sense of fear before something important that was about to happen. The countess looked at Prince Andrei with sad and gravely stern eyes when he spoke with Natasha, and timidly and with feigned casualness began some trivial conversation as soon as he glanced at her. Sonya was afraid to leave Natasha and afraid of being in the way when she was with them. Natasha turned pale with the fear of expectation whenever she was left alone with him for a moment. Prince Andrei astonished her with his timidity. She felt that he needed to tell her something, but that he could not bring himself to do so.

When Prince Andrei left that evening, the countess went up to Natasha and said in a whisper:

“Well?”

“Mama, for God’s sake, don’t ask me anything now. It cannot be spoken of,” said Natasha.

But despite that, Natasha spent a long time that evening lying in her mother’s bed, now agitated, now frightened, her eyes becoming fixed. At one moment she told her how he had praised her; then how he had said that he would go abroad; then that he had asked where they would be living that summer; then how he had asked her about Boris.

“But nothing like this, like this... has ever happened to me!” she said. “Only I am frightened when I am with him; I am always frightened when I am with him. What does that mean? It means that this is the real thing, doesn’t it? Mama, are you asleep?”

“No, my darling, I am frightened myself,” her mother replied. “Go.”

“I won’t sleep anyway. What nonsense it is to sleep! Mama, Mama, nothing like this has ever happened to me!” she said, in wonder and alarm at the feeling of which she was conscious within herself. “And could we ever have imagined it!...”

It seemed to Natasha that she had fallen in love with Prince Andrei the very first time she saw him at Otradnoye. She seemed frightened by this strange, unexpected happiness: that the very man she had chosen even then (she was firmly convinced of this) had now met her again and, it seemed, was not indifferent to her. “And he had to come to Petersburg now, of all times, when we are here. And we had to meet at that ball. All this is fate. It is clear that this is fate, that all of it has been leading to this. Even then, the moment I saw him, I felt something special.”

“What else did he say to you? What are those verses? Read them...” her mother said thoughtfully, asking about the verses Prince Andrei had written in Natasha’s album.

“Mama, it isn’t shameful that he is a widower, is it?”

“That will do, Natasha. Pray to God. Marriages are made in heaven.”

“My darling Mama, how I love you, how happy I am!” Natasha cried, weeping tears of happiness and agitation and embracing her mother.

At that very time Prince Andrei was sitting with Pierre and telling him of his love for Natasha and of his firm resolve to marry her.
