Pierre had been downstairs, had walked through the drawing rooms, and had struck all the guests with his preoccupied, distracted, and gloomy appearance.

Ever since the ball, Pierre had felt attacks of melancholy approaching and had tried with desperate effort to struggle against them. Since the prince had become close to his wife, Pierre had unexpectedly been appointed a chamberlain, and from that time on he began to feel burdened and ashamed in high society, and his former gloomy thoughts about the futility of all human things began to come to him more often. At the same time, the feeling he had noticed between Natasha, his protégée, and Prince Andrei, by the contrast between his own position and that of his friend, intensified this gloomy mood still further. He tried equally to avoid thoughts of his wife and of Natasha and Prince Andrei. Again everything seemed insignificant to him in comparison with eternity; again the question presented itself: “What for?” And day and night he forced himself to work on Masonic writings, hoping to drive away the approaching evil spirit. At eleven o’clock, having left the countess’s apartments, Pierre was sitting upstairs in his own low, smoke-filled room, wearing a threadbare dressing gown and copying out the authentic Scottish statutes, when someone entered his room. It was Prince Andrei.

“Ah, it is you,” said Pierre with a distracted and displeased look. “And here I am, working,” he said, pointing to the notebook with that expression of seeking refuge from life’s adversities with which unhappy people look upon their work.

Prince Andrei, his face radiant, enraptured, and renewed to life, stopped before Pierre and, failing to notice his sad face, smiled at him with the selfishness of happiness.

“Well, my dear fellow,” he said, “I wanted to tell you yesterday, and I have come to you today for that very purpose. I have never experienced anything like it. I am in love, my friend.”

Pierre suddenly sighed heavily and let his ponderous body fall onto the sofa beside Prince Andrei.

“With Natasha Rostova, yes?” he said.

“Yes, yes; who else? I would never have believed it, but this feeling is stronger than I am. Yesterday I was tormented, I suffered, but I would not give up that torment for anything in the world. I did not live before. Only now am I alive, but I cannot live without her. But can she love me?... I am old for her... Why don’t you say anything?...”

“I? I? What did I tell you?” Pierre suddenly said, rising and beginning to pace the room. “I always thought so... That girl is such a treasure, such a... She is a rare girl... My dear friend, I beg you, do not reason too much, do not doubt; marry, marry, and marry... And I am certain that there will be no happier man than you.”

“But she?”

“She loves you.”

“Don’t talk nonsense...” said Prince Andrei, smiling and looking into Pierre’s eyes.

“She loves you, I know she does,” Pierre shouted angrily.

“No, listen,” said Prince Andrei, stopping him by taking his hand. “Do you know what position I am in? I need to tell someone everything.”

Pierre, in reply to Natasha’s words, told her how unbearable it had been for him in Petersburg to attend evening parties and dinners with ladies.

“I have quite forgotten how to talk to ladies,” he said. “It is simply boring. Especially since I was so busy.”

Natasha looked intently at him and continued:

“Marie is such a delight!” she said. “How well she understands children. It is as though she sees only their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitenka began to be capricious...”

“Oh, how like his father he is,” Pierre interrupted.

Natasha understood why he had made this remark about Mitenka’s resemblance to Nikolai: the memory of his dispute with his brother-in-law was unpleasant to him, and he wanted to know Natasha’s opinion of it.

“Nikolenka has this weakness: if something is not accepted by everyone, he will not agree to it for anything. But I understand that what you particularly value is opening up a new path,” she said, repeating words Pierre had once spoken.

“No, the main thing,” said Pierre, “is that, for Nikolai, ideas and reasoning are an amusement, almost a way of passing the time. There he is building up a library and has made it a rule not to buy a new book before he has read the one he bought—Sismondi, and Rousseau, and Montesquieu,” Pierre added with a smile. “You know how I...” he began, intending to soften his words; but Natasha interrupted him, making it clear that this was unnecessary.

“So you say that, for him, ideas are an amusement...”

“Yes, while for me everything else is an amusement. The whole time I was in Petersburg, I saw everyone as though in a dream. When an idea occupies me, everything else is an amusement.”

“Oh, what a pity I did not see you greeting the children,” said Natasha. “Which of them was happiest to see you? Liza, surely?”

“Yes,” said Pierre, and continued with what occupied his mind. “Nikolai says that we must not think. But I cannot help it. Quite apart from the fact that in Petersburg I felt—I can tell you this—that without me all of it was falling apart, with everyone pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and then my idea is so simple and clear. You see, I am not saying that we ought to oppose this person or that person. We may be mistaken. What I say is: let those who love the good join hands, and let there be one banner—active virtue. Prince Sergei is a splendid man and clever.”

Natasha would not have doubted that Pierre’s idea was a great idea, but one thing troubled her. It was that he was her husband. “Can such an important and necessary man for society also be my husband? I

The subject of history is the life of peoples and of humanity. To grasp directly and encompass in words—to describe—the life not merely of humanity, but even of a single people, appears impossible.

Earlier historians often employed one simple device in order to describe and grasp the seemingly elusive life of a people. They described the activity of individual men who ruled the people; and for them, that activity expressed the activity of the entire people.

To the questions of how individual men compelled peoples to act according to their will, and what governed the will of those men themselves, historians answered the first question by acknowledging the will of the Deity, which subjected peoples to the will of one chosen man, and the second question by acknowledging the same Deity, which directed the will of the chosen man toward its predestined goal.

Thus these questions were resolved through faith in the direct participation of the Deity in the affairs of humanity.

The new science of history has, in theory, rejected both of these propositions.

It would seem that, having rejected the beliefs of the ancients concerning the subordination of men to the Deity and the definite goal toward which peoples are led, the new science should have studied not the manifestations of power but the causes that produce it. But it has not done so. Having rejected in theory the views of earlier historians, it follows them in practice.

In place of men endowed with divine power and directly guided by the will of the Deity, modern history has put either heroes endowed with extraordinary, superhuman abilities, or simply men of the most varied qualities, from monarchs to journalists, who guide the masses. In place of the former goals of the Jewish, Greek, and Roman peoples—goals pleasing to the Deity—which to the ancients appeared to be the goals of humanity’s movement, modern history has put its own goals: the welfare of the French, German, and English peoples and, at its highest level of abstraction, the welfare of the civilization of all humanity, by which are usually meant the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of a large continent.

“Yes, love,” he thought again with perfect clarity, “but not the love that loves for something, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love I experienced for the first time when, dying, I saw my enemy and loved him all the same. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and which needs no object. Even now I experience this blissful feeling. To love one’s neighbors, to love one’s enemies. To love everything—to love God in all His manifestations. One can love a dear person with human love; but only an enemy can be loved with divine love. And that was why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?... Loving with human love, one can pass from love to hatred; but divine love cannot change. Nothing, not death, nothing can destroy it. It is the essence of the soul. And how many people I have hated in my life. And of all people, I have loved and hated no one more than her.” And he vividly pictured Natasha to himself, not as he had pictured her before, with only her charm, which gave him joy; but for the first time he pictured her soul. And he understood her feelings, her sufferings, her shame, her remorse. Now, for the first time, he understood all the cruelty of his refusal, saw the cruelty of his break with her. “If only it were possible for me to see her just once more. Once, looking into those eyes, to say...”

And piti-piti-piti and ti-ti, and piti-piti—boom, the fly struck... And his attention was suddenly transferred to another world, a world of reality and delirium, in which something extraordinary was taking place. In that world, the building still went on rising without collapsing; something still stretched out; the candle with the red circle still burned; the same sphinx-shirt lay by the door; but besides all this, something creaked, a breath of fresh wind blew in, and a new white sphinx, standing upright, appeared before the door. And in the head of that sphinx were the pale face and shining eyes of that very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

“Oh, how oppressive this unceasing delirium is!” Prince Andrei thought, trying to banish that face from his imagination. But the face stood before him with the force of reality, and the face drew nearer. Prince Andrei wanted to return to the former world of pure thought, but he could not, and the delirium drew him into its realm. The soft, whispering voice continued its measured babble; something pressed, something stretched out, and the strange face stood before him.

Prince Andrei gathered all his strength to recover his senses; he moved, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, his eyes grew dim, and, like a man plunged into water, he lost consciousness. When he came to, Natasha, that same living Natasha whom, of all the people in the world, he most wished to love with that new, pure, divine love that had now been revealed to him, was kneeling before him. He understood that this was the living, real Natasha, and was not surprised, but quietly rejoiced. Natasha, on her knees, looked at him in fright but as though transfixed (she could not move), holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and motionless. Only in its lower part did something tremble.

Prince Andrei sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.

“You?” he said. “How happy this is!”

With a quick but careful movement, Natasha moved toward him on her knees and, carefully taking his hand, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.

“Forgive me!” she said in a whisper, raising her head and looking at him. “Forgive me!”

“I love you,” said Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me...”

“What is there to forgive?” asked Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me for what I d-did,” Natasha uttered in a barely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more and more rapidly, barely touching it with her lips.

“I love you more, better than before,” said Prince Andrei, raising her face with his hand so that he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, brimming with happy tears, looked at him timidly, compassionately, and with joyful love. Natasha’s thin, pale face with its swollen lips was more than unattractive; it was frightening. But Prince Andrei did not see that face; he saw the radiant eyes, which were beautiful. Voices were heard behind them.

Pyotr the valet, now fully awake, woke the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything that was happening and, carefully covering his undressed body with a sheet, huddled on the bench.

“What is this?” said the doctor, raising himself from his bed. “Be so good as to leave, madam.”

At that same moment, a girl sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter’s absence, was knocking at the door.

Like a somnambulist awakened in the middle of her sleep, Natasha left the room and, on returning to her own hut, fell sobbing onto her bed.

From that day onward, throughout the rest of the Rostovs’ journey, at every halt and overnight stop, Natasha did not leave the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected either such fortitude or such skill in tending a wounded man from a young lady.

However dreadful the thought seemed to the countess that Prince Andrei might—very probably, according to the doctor—die on the journey in her daughter’s arms, she could not oppose Natasha. Although, as a result of the closeness now established between the wounded Prince Andrei and Natasha, it occurred to them that, in the event of his recovery, their former relationship as betrothed man and woman would be renewed, no one, and least of all Natasha and Prince Andrei, spoke of it: the unresolved, looming question of life or death, not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, obscured all other suppositions.

XXXIII.

Pierre awoke late on September 3. His head ached; the clothes in which he had slept without undressing weighed upon his body, and in his soul was a vague awareness of something shameful committed the day before; that shameful thing was yesterday’s conversation with Captain Ramballe.

The clock showed eleven, but outside it seemed particularly overcast. Pierre got up, rubbed his eyes, and, seeing the pistol with the carved stock that Gerasim had put back on the writing desk, Pierre remembered where he was and what lay before him on that very day.

“Can I already be too late?” thought Pierre. “No, he will probably make his entry into Moscow no earlier than twelve.” Pierre did not allow himself to reflect on what lay before him, but hurried to act as soon as possible.

Having straightened his clothes, Pierre took the pistol in his hands and was already preparing to leave. But then, for the first time, the thought occurred to him of how he was to carry this weapon—not openly in his hand—through the streets. Even under his broad caftan, it was difficult to conceal the large pistol. It could not be placed inconspicuously either behind his belt or under his arm. Besides, the pistol was unloaded, and Pierre had not had time to load it. “The dagger will do just as well,” Pierre told himself, though, when discussing the execution of his intention, he had more than once concluded that the chief mistake of the student in 1809 had been that he had wanted to kill Napoleon with a dagger. But as though Pierre’s chief aim were not to carry out his intended deed, but to prove to himself that he was not renouncing his intention and was doing everything to carry it out, Pierre hurriedly took the blunt, notched dagger in a green sheath that he had bought by the Sukharev Tower together with the pistol, and concealed it under his waistcoat.

But after that night in Mytishchi, when, in a half-delirium, the woman he longed for appeared before him and when, pressing her hand to his lips, he wept quiet, joyful tears, love for one woman imperceptibly stole into his heart and bound him to life again. Both joyful and anxious thoughts began to come to him. Recalling that moment at the dressing station when he had seen Kuragin, he could no longer return to that feeling: he was now tormented by the question of whether he was alive. And he did not dare ask.

His illness followed its physical course, but what Natasha called “this happened to him” occurred two days before Princess Marya’s arrival. It was that last moral struggle between life and death in which death was victorious. It was the unexpected realization that he still cherished life, which appeared to him in his love for Natasha, and a final, vanquished fit of terror before the unknown.

It was evening. As usual after dinner, he was in a mildly feverish state, and his thoughts were extraordinarily clear. Sonya was sitting at the table. He dozed off. Suddenly a feeling of happiness enveloped him.

“Ah, she has come in!” he thought.

Indeed, in Sonya’s place sat Natasha, who had just entered with inaudible steps.

Ever since she had begun tending him, he had always experienced this physical sensation of her nearness. She sat in an armchair, turned sideways to him, shielding the candlelight from him with her body, and knitted a stocking.

(She had learned to knit stockings after Prince Andrei once told her that no one knew how to tend the sick as well as old nurses who knitted stockings, and that there was something soothing in knitting a stocking.) Her slender fingers rapidly worked the needles, which occasionally clicked against each other, and the pensive profile of her lowered face was clearly visible to him. She made a movement—the ball rolled off her knees. She started, glanced at him, and, shielding the candle with her hand, bent with a careful, supple, precise movement, picked up the ball, and sat down in her former position.

He looked at her without moving and saw that after her movement she needed to draw a full breath, but she did not dare do so and breathed carefully.

At the Trinity Lavra they had spoken of the past, and he had told her that if he lived, he would thank God forever for his wound, which had brought him together with her again; but since then they had never spoken of the future.

“Could it or could it not have been?” he now thought, looking at her and listening to the light metallic sound of the needles. “Can it really be that fate brought me together with her so strangely only for me to die? Can it really be that the truth of life was revealed to me only so that I might live a lie? I love her more than anything in the world. But what am I to do if I love her?” he said, and suddenly, involuntarily, he groaned, from a habit he had acquired during his sufferings.

Hearing the sound, Natasha put down the stocking, leaned closer to him, and suddenly, noticing his shining eyes, went up to him with a light step and bent over him.

“Are you not asleep?”

“No, I have been looking at you for a long time; I felt it when you came in. No one gives me, as you do, that gentle stillness... that light. I feel so much like weeping for joy.”

Natasha moved closer to him. Her face shone with rapturous joy.

“Natasha, I love you too much. More than anything in the world.”

“And I?” She turned away for a moment. “Why too much?” she said.

“Why too much?... Well, what do you think, what do you feel in your soul, in your whole soul—will I live? What does it seem to you?”

“I am sure, I am sure!” Natasha almost cried out, taking both his hands with a passionate movement.

He was silent for a while.

“How good that would be!” And, taking her hand, he kissed it.

Natasha was happy and agitated; and at once she remembered that this was not allowed, that he needed quiet.

“But you have not slept,” she said, suppressing her joy. “Try to fall asleep... please.”

He released her hand after pressing it, and she moved over to the candle and again sat down in her former position. Twice she looked back at him; his eyes shone in response to hers. She assigned herself a certain amount of the stocking and told herself that she would not look back until she had finished it.

Indeed, soon afterward he closed his eyes and fell asleep. He did not sleep long and suddenly awoke anxiously, in a cold sweat.

As he fell asleep, he kept thinking about the same thing he had been thinking about all that time—about life and death. And more about death. He felt himself closer to it.

“Love? What is love?” he thought.

“Love stands in the way of death. Love is life. Everything, everything I understand, I understand only because I love. Everything is, everything exists, only because I love. Everything is bound together by love alone. Love is God, and to die means for me, a particle of love, to return to the universal and eternal source.” These thoughts seemed comforting to him. But they were only thoughts. Something was lacking in them; there was something one-sidedly personal and intellectual—there was no certainty. And there was the same uneasiness and obscurity. He fell asleep.

He dreamed that he was lying in the same room in which he was actually lying, but that he was not wounded and was healthy. Many different faces, insignificant and indifferent, appeared before Prince Andrei. He talked with them, argued about something unnecessary. They were preparing to go somewhere. Prince Andrei vaguely remembered that all this was insignificant and that he had other, more important concerns, but he continued talking, astonishing them with empty, witty words. Little by little, imperceptibly, all these faces began to disappear, and everything was replaced by a single question concerning the closed door. He got up and went to the door to slide the bolt and lock it. Everything depended on whether or not he managed to lock it. He walked, he hurried, but his legs would not move, and he knew that he would not manage to lock the door, yet he still painfully strained all his strength. And a tormenting fear seized him. And this fear was the fear of death: it was standing behind the door. But at the very moment when he was crawling helplessly and awkwardly toward the door, that dreadful something, already pressing from the other side, was forcing its way through it. Something not human—death—was forcing its way through the door, and he had to hold it back. He seized the door and strained in a final effort—it was no longer possible to lock it—at least to hold it shut; but his strength was weak and clumsy, and, pressed by the dreadful thing, the door opened and closed again.

Once more it pressed from the other side. His last, superhuman efforts were in vain, and both halves opened soundlessly. It entered, and it was death. And Prince Andrei died.

“Well!...” said the old count, spreading his hands, and sank helplessly onto the sofa.

“What is to be done! Who has not had such a thing happen to him?” said the son in a casual, bold tone, while in his heart he considered himself a scoundrel, a blackguard who could not atone for his crime with his whole life. He would have liked to kiss his father’s hands and, on his knees, beg his forgiveness, but in a careless and even coarse tone he said that such a thing happened to everyone.

Count Ilya Andreich lowered his eyes on hearing these words from his son and began bustling about, looking for something.

“Yes, yes,” he said, “it will be difficult, I’m afraid, difficult to obtain... who hasn’t had it happen! Yes, who hasn’t had it happen...” And the count cast a fleeting glance at his son’s face and walked out of the room... Nikolai had been preparing to meet resistance, but had never expected this.

“Papa! Pa...pa!” he cried after him, sobbing. “Forgive me!” And, seizing his father’s hand, he pressed his lips to it and began to weep.

While the father was having his explanation with his son, an explanation of no less importance was taking place between the mother and daughter. Natasha ran excitedly to her mother.

“Mamma!... Mamma!... he has made me...”

“Made you what?”

“Made, made a proposal. Mamma! Mamma!” she cried.

The countess could not believe her ears. Denisov had made a proposal. To whom? To this tiny little girl Natasha, who had so recently played with dolls and was still taking lessons even now.

“Natasha, stop it, what nonsense!” she said, still hoping it was a joke.

“There, you see—nonsense! I’m telling you something serious,” Natasha said angrily. “I came to ask what I should do, and you tell me, ‘Nonsense’...”

The countess shrugged her shoulders.

“If it is true that Monsieur Denisov has proposed to you, then tell him that he is a fool, and that is all.”

“No, he is not a fool,” Natasha said seriously, taking offense.

“Well, then, what do you want? You are all in love nowadays, after all. Well, if you are in love, then marry him,” said the countess with an angry laugh. “God be with you!”

“No, Mamma, I am not in love with him; I must not be in love with him.”

“Well, then, tell him just that.”

“Mamma, are you angry? You aren’t angry, darling, are you? How is it my fault?”

“No, but what is it, my dear? If you like, I will go and tell him,” said the countess, smiling.

“No, I’ll do it myself; only teach me how. Everything is easy for you,” she added, responding to her smile. “And if only you had seen how he said it to me! I know that he did not mean to say it, but he said it accidentally in spite of himself.”

“Well, you must refuse him all the same.”

“No, I mustn’t. I feel so sorry for him! He is so sweet.”

“Well, then, accept the proposal. It is high time you were married anyway,” her mother said angrily and mockingly.

“No, Mamma, I feel so sorry for him. I don’t know how I shall say it.”

“You do not need to say anything; I will tell him myself,” said the countess, indignant that anyone had dared to look upon this little Natasha as a grown woman.

“No, not for anything; I’ll do it myself, and you listen at the door.” And Natasha ran through the drawing room into the hall, where Denisov sat on the same chair by the clavichord, his face covered by his hands. He sprang up at the sound of her light footsteps.

“Natalie,” he said, approaching her with quick steps, “decide my fate. It is in your hands!”

“Vasily Dmitrich, I feel so sorry for you!... No, but you are so wonderful... but it must not be... this... but I shall always love you all the same.”

Denisov bent over her hand, and she heard strange sounds that she could not understand. She kissed him on his black, tangled, curly head. At that moment the hurried rustling of the countess’s dress could be heard. She approached them.

“Vasily Dmitrich, I thank you for the honor,” said the countess in an embarrassed voice, which nevertheless seemed stern to Denisov, “but my daughter is so young, and I thought that, as my son’s friend, you would address yourself to me first. In that case you would not have placed me under the necessity of refusing.”

“Countess...” said Denisov with downcast eyes and a guilty look; he tried to say something more and faltered.

Natasha could not calmly see him looking so pitiful. She began to sob loudly.

“Countess, I am guilty before you,” Denisov continued in a breaking voice, “but know that I so idolize your daughter and your whole family that I would give two lives...” He looked at the countess and, noticing her stern face... “Well, farewell, Countess,” he said, kissing her hand, and, without looking at Natasha, walked out of the room with quick, resolute steps.

The next day Rostov saw Denisov off, as he did not wish to remain in Moscow another single day. All his Moscow friends held a farewell for Denisov at the gypsies’, and he did not remember how they put him into the sleigh or how he was driven through the first three posting stations.

After Denisov’s departure, Rostov, while waiting for the money that the old count could not raise at once, spent another two weeks in Moscow without leaving the house, and chiefly in the young ladies’ room.

Sonya was more tender and devoted to him than before. She seemed to want to show him that his gambling loss had been a heroic deed for which she now loved him even more; but Nikolai now considered himself unworthy of her.

He filled the girls’ albums with verses and music, and, without taking leave of any of his acquaintances, having at last sent all forty-three thousand and received Dolokhov’s receipt, he left at the end of November to catch up with the regiment, which was already in Poland.

PART TWO

After his explanation with his wife, Pierre set out for Petersburg. There were no horses at the posting station in Torzhok, or else the stationmaster did not want to provide them. Pierre had to wait. Without undressing, he lay down on a leather sofa before a round table, placed his large feet in their warm boots on the table, and sank into thought.

“Would you like the trunks brought in? Shall I make up a bed? Would you like some tea?” asked the valet.

Pierre did not answer, because he heard and saw nothing. He had become lost in thought at the previous station and continued thinking about the same thing—about something so important that he paid no attention at all to what was happening around him. Not only was he uninterested in whether he would arrive in Petersburg sooner or later, or whether there would or would not be a place for him to rest at this station, but, in comparison with the thoughts that now occupied him, it was all the same to him whether he would remain at this station for several hours or for his whole life.

The stationmaster, the stationmaster’s wife, the valet, and a peasant woman with Torzhok embroidery came into the room, offering their services. Without changing the position of his upraised legs, Pierre looked at them through his spectacles and did not understand what they could possibly need or how they could all live without having resolved the questions that occupied him. And he had been occupied by the very same questions ever since the day when, after the duel, he returned from Sokolniki and spent the first agonizing, sleepless night; only now, in the solitude of the journey, they took possession of him with particular force. At the end of December, in a black woolen dress, her braid carelessly tied in a knot, thin and pale, Natasha sat with her feet tucked up in the corner of the sofa, tensely crumpling and releasing the ends of her sash, and gazed at the corner of the door.

She was gazing toward where he had gone, to that other side of life. And that side of life, of which she had never thought before, which had previously seemed so distant and incredible to her, was now closer and dearer to her, more comprehensible, than this side of life, in which everything was either emptiness and destruction, or suffering and humiliation.

She gazed toward where she knew he was; but she could not see him otherwise than as he had been here. She saw him again just as he had been in Mytishchi, at Troitsa, in Yaroslavl.

She saw his face, heard his voice, and repeated his words and her own words spoken to him, and sometimes invented for herself and for him new words that might have been said then.

There he is, lying in an armchair in his little velvet coat, resting his head on his thin, pale hand. His chest is terribly sunken and his shoulders raised. His lips are firmly compressed, his eyes gleam, and a wrinkle springs up and vanishes on his pale forehead. One of his legs is trembling rapidly, almost imperceptibly. Natasha knows that he is struggling with agonizing pain. “What is this pain? Why pain? What does he feel? How does it hurt him?” Natasha thinks. He noticed her attention, raised his eyes, and, without smiling, began to speak.

“One thing is terrible,” he said. “It is to bind oneself forever to a suffering person. It is eternal torment.” And he looked at her with a searching gaze. Natasha, as always, answered then before she had time to think about what she was answering; she said: “It cannot go on like this, it will not; you will get well—completely.”

She now saw him again and now relived everything she had felt then. She remembered his long, sad, stern gaze at those words and understood the meaning of reproach and despair in that prolonged gaze.

“I agreed,” Natasha now said to herself, “that it would be terrible if he were always to remain suffering. I said it then only because it would have been terrible for him, but he understood it differently. He thought it would have been terrible for me. Even then he still wanted to live—he was afraid of death. And I said it to him so crudely, so stupidly. I did not mean that. I meant something entirely different. If I had said what I meant, I would have said: even if he were dying, were dying all the time before my eyes, I would be happy compared with what I am now. Now... There is nothing, no one. Did he know that? No. He did not know and never will know. And now it can never, never be put right.” And again he said the same words to her, but now, in her imagination, Natasha answered him differently. She stopped him and said: “Terrible for you, but not for me. You must know that without you there is nothing in life for me, and to suffer with you is the greatest happiness for me.” And he took her hand and pressed it as he had pressed it on that terrible evening, four days before his death. And in her imagination she said to him still other tender, loving words that she could have said then. “I love you... you... I love you, I love you...” she said, convulsively clasping her hands, clenching her teeth with fierce effort.

And sweet sorrow enfolded her, and tears were already coming into her eyes, but suddenly she asked herself: to whom was she saying this? Where was he, and who was he now? And again everything was veiled by dry, unyielding bewilderment, and again, tensely drawing her brows together, she peered toward where he was. And now, any moment, it seemed to her, she would penetrate the mystery... But at the very moment when the incomprehensible seemed about to be revealed to her, the loud rattle of the door’s latch struck painfully on her hearing. Quickly and incautiously, with a frightened expression on her face that had nothing to do with Natasha, the maid Dunyasha entered the room.

“Please come to Papa, quickly,” Dunyasha said with a peculiar, animated expression. “A misfortune, concerning Pyotr Ilyich... a letter,” she uttered with a sob.

II.

Besides a general feeling of estrangement from all people, Natasha at that time experienced a special feeling of estrangement from the members of her family. All her own people—her father, her mother, Sonya—were so close to her, so familiar, so commonplace, that all their words and feelings seemed to her an insult to the world in which she had lately been living, and she was not only indifferent to them, but looked at them with hostility. She heard Dunyasha’s words, about Pyotr Ilyich, about a misfortune, but did not understand them.

“What sort of misfortune can they have, what misfortune could there be? Everything with them is the same old, familiar, peaceful thing,” Natasha said inwardly.

When she entered the hall, her father was hurrying out of the countess’s room. His face was crumpled and wet with tears. He had evidently run out of that room to give free rein to the sobs that were choking him. On seeing Natasha, he flung up his hands in despair and burst into painful, convulsive sobs that distorted his round, gentle face.

“Pe... Petya... Go, go, she... she... is calling...” And, weeping like a child and rapidly shuffling on his weakened legs, he went to a chair and almost fell onto it, covering his face with his hands.

Suddenly it was as though an electric current ran through Natasha’s whole being. Something struck her heart with terrible pain. She felt an awful pain; it seemed to her that something was being torn away inside her and that she was dying. But immediately after the pain she felt an instantaneous release from the prohibition against life that had lain upon her. On seeing her father and hearing her mother’s terrible, harsh scream from behind the door, she instantly forgot herself and her own grief. She ran up to her father, but he, waving his hand feebly, pointed toward her mother’s door. Princess Marya, pale, her lower jaw trembling, came out through the door and took Natasha by the hand, saying something to her. Natasha neither saw nor heard her. She went quickly through the door, stopped for an instant as though struggling with herself, and ran up to her mother.

The countess lay in an armchair, stretched out in a strangely awkward position, and beat her head against the wall. Sonya and the maids held her by the arms.

“Natasha, Natasha!..” cried the countess. “It isn’t true, it isn’t true... He is lying... Natasha!” she cried, pushing away those around her. “All of you go away, it isn’t true! Killed!.. Ha, ha, ha!.. It isn’t true!”

Natasha put one knee on the armchair, bent over her mother, embraced her, lifted her with unexpected strength, turned her face toward herself, and pressed close to her.

“Mamma!.. my darling!.. I’m here, my dear. Mamma,” she whispered to her, without falling silent for a single second.

“Ice cream, only you won’t be given any,” said Marya Dmitrievna.

Natasha saw that there was nothing to be afraid of, and so she was not afraid of Marya Dmitrievna either.

“Marya Dmitrievna? What kind of ice cream? I don’t like cream ice cream.”

“Carrot.”

“No, what kind? Marya Dmitrievna, what kind?” she almost shouted. “I want to know!”

Marya Dmitrievna and the countess laughed, and all the guests followed them. Everyone laughed not at Marya Dmitrievna’s answer, but at the incomprehensible boldness and adroitness of this little girl, who knew how and dared to address Marya Dmitrievna in such a way.

Natasha desisted only when she was told that there would be pineapple ice cream. Champagne was served before the ice cream. The music began playing again, the count kissed his dear countess, and the guests rose and congratulated the countess, clinked glasses across the table with the count, the children, and one another. Once again the waiters began bustling about, the chairs clattered, and in the same order, but with redder faces, the guests returned to the drawing room and the count’s study.

XVII.

The Boston tables were unfolded, parties were formed, and the count’s guests settled themselves in the two drawing rooms, the sofa room, and the library.

The count, spreading his cards out in a fan, could barely restrain himself from his habitual after-dinner nap and laughed at everything. The young people, urged on by the countess, gathered around the clavichord and the harp. Julie, at everyone’s request, was the first to play a little piece with variations on the harp, and then joined the other young ladies in asking Natasha and Nikolai, who were known for their musicality, to sing something. Natasha, who had been addressed as though she were grown up, was visibly very proud of this, but at the same time felt shy.

“What shall we sing?” she asked.

“‘The Brook,’” Nikolai replied.

“Well, let’s do it quickly. Boris, come here,” said Natasha. “But where is Sonya?”

She looked around and, seeing that her friend was not in the room, ran off to find her.

Running into Sonya’s room and not finding her friend there, Natasha ran through to the nursery—and Sonya was not there either. Natasha realized that Sonya was in the corridor, on the trunk. The trunk in the corridor was the place of sorrows for the younger female generation of the Rostov household. And indeed Sonya, in her airy pink dress, crushing it beneath her, lay facedown on the dirty striped feather bed belonging to the nurse, atop the trunk, and, covering her face with her little fingers, sobbed violently, her bare little shoulders trembling. Natasha’s face, animated and festive all day for her name day, suddenly changed: her eyes became fixed, then her broad neck quivered and the corners of her lips drooped.

“Sonya! What is it?… What, what’s the matter with you? Oo-oo-oo!…”

And Natasha, opening her large mouth wide and becoming completely ugly, began bawling like a child, not knowing the reason and only because Sonya was crying. Sonya tried to raise her head, tried to answer, but could not and hid herself still more deeply. Natasha wept, sitting down on the blue feather bed and embracing her friend. Gathering her strength, Sonya raised herself a little, began wiping away her tears, and started to tell her.

“Nikolenka is leaving in a week, his… paper… has come through… he told me himself… But I wouldn’t cry at all… (she showed the little sheet of paper she was holding in her hand: they were verses written by Nikolai) I wouldn’t cry at all, but you can’t… no one can understand… what a soul he has.”

And she began crying again because his soul was so good.

“It’s all right for you… I’m not envious… I love you, and Boris too,” she said, having gathered a little strength. “He’s sweet… there are no obstacles for you. But Nikolai is my cousin… it would take… the Metropolitan himself… and even then it can’t be done. And then, if Mamma… (Sonya both regarded and called the countess her mother)… she will say that I’m ruining Nikolai’s career, that I have no heart, that I’m ungrateful, but truly… by God… (she crossed herself) I love her so much, and all of you too; only Vera… Why? What have I done to her? I’m so grateful to all of you that I would gladly sacrifice everything, but I have nothing to sacrifice…”

Sonya could say no more and once again hid her head in her hands and the feather bed. Natasha was beginning to calm down, but her face showed that she understood the full gravity of her friend’s sorrow.

“Sonya!” she said suddenly, as though she had guessed the true cause of her cousin’s distress. “Vera spoke to you after dinner, didn’t she? Yes?”

“Yes, Nikolai wrote these verses himself, and I copied out some others too; she found them on my table and said that she would show them to Mamma, and she also said that I was ungrateful, that Mamma would never allow him to marry me, and that he would marry Julie. You see how he is with her all day… Natasha! Why?…”

And once again she began crying more bitterly than before. Natasha raised her up, embraced her, and, smiling through her tears, began to comfort her.

“Sonya, don’t believe her, darling, don’t believe her. Do you remember how the three of us talked with Nikolenka in the sofa room; remember, after supper? Why, we settled everything, how it would be. I no longer remember how, but do you remember how everything was all right and everything was possible? Why, Uncle Shinshin’s brother is married to his first cousin, and we’re only second cousins. And Boris said that it’s quite possible. You know, I told him everything. And he’s so clever and so good,” Natasha said. “Sonya, don’t cry, my precious darling, sweetheart, Sonya.” And she kissed her, laughing. “Vera is wicked, God be with her! But everything will be all right, and she won’t tell Mamma; Nikolenka will tell her himself, and he hasn’t even thought about Julie.”

And she kissed her on the head. Sonya raised herself, and the little kitten came back to life, her little eyes began to sparkle, and it seemed that at any moment she was ready to flick her tail, spring up on her soft paws, and begin playing with the ball of yarn again, as was proper for her.

“You think so? Truly? By God?” she said, quickly straightening her dress and hair.

“Truly, by God!” Natasha replied, tucking back beneath her friend’s braid a stray lock of coarse hair.

And they both laughed.

“Well, let’s go and sing ‘The Brook.’”

“Let’s go.”

“And you know, that fat Pierre who was sitting opposite me is so funny!” Natasha said suddenly, stopping. “I’m having such fun!”

And Natasha ran down the corridor.

Sonya, brushing off the down and hiding the verses in the bosom of her dress, beside her little neck where the bones of her chest protruded, ran after Natasha down the corridor into the sofa room with light, cheerful steps and a flushed face. At the guests’ request the young people sang the quartet ‘The Brook,’ which everyone liked very much; then Nikolai sang a song he had recently learned:

On a pleasant night, by moonlight,

How happy to imagine

That there is someone else in the world

Who thinks of you as well!

That she too, with her lovely hand,

Wandering over the golden harp,

With her passionate harmony

“And you?…” he said, turning to Dolokhov. No sooner had he asked this than he realized that it should not have been asked.

“Yes, perhaps…” Dolokhov replied coldly and angrily. He glanced at Sonya and, frowning, looked at Nikolai again with exactly the same expression with which he had looked at Pierre at the club dinner.

“There is something going on,” Nikolai thought, and he was confirmed still further in this supposition by the fact that Dolokhov left immediately after dinner. He called Natasha and asked what it was.

“I was looking for you,” Natasha said, running out to him. “I told you, but you would never believe me,” she said triumphantly. “He proposed to Sonya.”

Little as Nikolai had concerned himself with Sonya during this time, something seemed to tear loose within him when he heard this. Dolokhov was a respectable and, in some respects, brilliant match for the orphan Sonya, who had no dowry. From the old countess’s point of view, and that of society, he could not be refused. And so Nikolai’s first feeling when he heard this was anger against Sonya. He prepared to say, “And a very good thing too; of course she must forget childhood promises and accept the proposal”; but before he had time to say it…

“Can you imagine! She refused him, refused him outright!” Natasha began. “She said she loved someone else,” she added after a short pause.

“My Sonya could not have acted otherwise!” Nikolai thought.

“No matter how much Mama begged her, she refused, and I know she will not change her mind once she has said something…”

“And Mama begged her!” Nikolai said reproachfully.

“Yes,” Natasha said. “You know, Nikolenka, don’t be angry; but I know you will not marry her. I know—God knows why—but I know for certain that you will not marry her.”

“Well, you cannot possibly know that,” Nikolai said. “But I must speak to her. What a darling Sonya is!” he added with a smile.

“She is such a darling! I’ll send her to you.” And Natasha kissed her brother and ran away.

A minute later Sonya entered, frightened, bewildered, and guilty. Nikolai went up to her and kissed her hand. This was the first time during this visit that they had spoken face to face and about their love.

“Sophie,” he said, timidly at first and then more and more boldly, “if you wish to refuse not merely a brilliant and advantageous match; but he is a splendid, noble man… he is my friend…”

Sonya interrupted him.

“I have already refused,” she said hastily.

“If you are refusing for my sake, I am afraid that the responsibility…”

Sonya interrupted him again. She looked at him with a frightened, imploring gaze.

“Nicolas, do not say that to me,” she said.

“No, I must. Perhaps it is conceit on my part, but it is better to say it. If you refuse him for my sake, then I must tell you the whole truth. I love you, I think, more than anyone…”

“That is enough for me,” Sonya said, flushing.

“No, but I have fallen in love a thousand times and will fall in love again, though I have no such feeling of friendship, trust, and love for anyone as I have for you. Besides, I am young. Maman does not want it. Well, quite simply, I promise nothing. And I ask you to think about Dolokhov’s proposal,” he said, pronouncing his friend’s surname with difficulty.

“Do not say that to me. I want nothing. I love you as a brother, and I always shall love you, and I need nothing more.”

“You are an angel; I am not worthy of you, but I am only afraid of deceiving you.” Nikolai kissed her hand once more.

XII

Iogel gave the merriest balls in Moscow. So said the mothers as they watched their adolescent daughters performing the steps they had only just learned; so said the adolescent girls and boys themselves, who danced until they dropped; so said the grown-up young ladies and young men who came to these balls intending to condescend to them and found in them the very best entertainment. That same year, two marriages resulted from these balls. Two pretty Princesses Gorchakov found suitors and married, thereby making the balls still more renowned. What was unusual about these balls was that there was neither host nor hostess: there was only the good-natured Iogel, flitting about like down and bowing and scraping according to all the rules of his art, who accepted lesson tickets from all his guests; and that only those who wanted to dance and enjoy themselves as thirteen- and fourteen-year-old girls do when putting on long dresses for the first time still attended these balls. With rare exceptions, everyone was, or appeared to be, pretty, so rapturously did they all smile and so brightly did their little eyes glow. Sometimes the best pupils even danced the shawl dance, and the best of them was Natasha, who was distinguished by her grace; but at this, the last ball, they danced only écossaises, anglaises, and the mazurka, which was just coming into fashion. Iogel had rented the ballroom in Bezukhov’s house, and the ball was a great success, as everyone said. There were many pretty girls, and the young Rostov ladies were among the prettiest. They were both especially happy and merry. That evening Sonya, proud of Dolokhov’s proposal, of her refusal, and of her explanation with Nikolai, had been whirling about even at home, not allowing the maid to finish braiding her hair, and now she glowed through and through with impetuous joy.

Natasha, no less proud that she was wearing a long dress for the first time and attending a real ball, was happier still. They wore white muslin dresses with pink ribbons.

Natasha fell in love from the very moment she entered the ball. She was not in love with anyone in particular, but she was in love with everyone. Whomever she was looking at at any given moment, she was in love with while she looked at him.

“Oh, how wonderful!” she kept saying, running up to Sonya.

Nikolai and Denisov walked through the rooms, surveying the dancers with kindly, patronizing looks.

“How sweet she is; she will be a beauty,” Denisov said.

“Who?”

“Countess Natasha,” Denisov replied.

“And how she dances—what grace!” he said again after a short pause.

“Yes, but whom are you talking about?”

“Your sister!” Denisov shouted angrily.

Rostov chuckled.

“My dear Count, you are one of my best pupils; you must dance,” little Iogel said, approaching Nikolai. “See how many pretty young ladies there are.” He addressed the same request to Denisov, who had also once been his pupil.

“No, my dear fellow, I shall be a wallflower,” Denisov said. “Do you not remember how poorly I profited from your lessons?…”

“Oh no!” Iogel said, hastening to reassure him. “You were merely inattentive, but you had ability; yes, you had ability.”

“All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are setting out for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg and, so it is said, intends himself to expose his precious life to the hazards of war. God grant that the Corsican monster, who is destroying the peace of Europe, may be struck down by the angel whom the Almighty, in His mercy, has given us as sovereign. Not to mention my brothers, this war has deprived me of a relationship most dear to my heart. I speak of young Nicholas Rostov, who, in his enthusiasm, could not endure inactivity and has left the university to enlist in the army. Well, dear Marie, I shall confess to you that, despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army has been a great sorrow to me. The young man of whom I spoke to you this summer has so much nobility, such genuine youth as one so rarely encounters in the age in which we live among our twenty-year-old old men. Above all, he has so much frankness and heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relations with him, however fleeting they may have been, have been one of the sweetest joys of my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. One day I shall tell you about our farewells and everything that was said as he was leaving. It is all still too fresh. Ah! dear friend, you are fortunate not to know these joys and these so poignant sorrows. You are fortunate, since the latter are usually the stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nicholas is too young ever to become anything more to me than a friend, but this sweet friendship, these so poetic and so pure relations, were a need of my heart. But let us speak of it no more. The great news of the day, which occupies all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Just imagine: the three princesses received very little, Prince Vasili nothing, and it is Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and, into the bargain, has been recognized as a legitimate son and consequently as Count Bezukhov and the possessor of the finest fortune in Russia. It is said that Prince Vasili played a very ugly part in this whole affair and that he went back to Petersburg quite crestfallen.

“I confess to you that I understand very little of all these matters of legacies and wills; what I do know is that, since the young man whom we all knew simply as Monsieur Pierre became Count Bezukhov and the possessor of one of the greatest fortunes in Russia, I have been greatly amused to observe the changes in the tone and manners of the mothers burdened with marriageable daughters, and of the young ladies themselves, toward this individual, who, incidentally, has always seemed to me a sorry fellow. Since for the past two years people have amused themselves by giving me prospective husbands whom, more often than not, I do not know, the matrimonial chronicle of Moscow is making me Countess Bezukhov. But you understand very well that I have no desire whatsoever to become her. Speaking of marriage, do you know that only very recently the aunt-in-general, Anna Mikhailovna, confided to me, under the seal of the greatest secrecy, a marriage plan for you? It is none other than Prince Vasili’s son Anatole, whom they would like to reform by marrying him to a rich and distinguished person, and it is upon you that the parents’ choice has fallen. I do not know how you will view the matter, but I thought it my duty to warn you of it. He is said to be very handsome and a very bad lot; that is all I have been able to learn about him.

“But enough chatter of this sort. I am finishing my second sheet, and Mamma has sent for me to go and dine at the Apraksins’. Read the mystical book I am sending you, which is all the rage among us. Although there are things in this book difficult for the feeble human understanding to grasp, it is an admirable book, the reading of which calms and elevates the soul. Farewell. My respects to your father and my compliments to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.

Julie.”

“P.S. Give me news of your brother and his charming little wife.”

The princess thought, smiled pensively—at which her face, illuminated by her radiant eyes, was completely transformed—and, suddenly rising slightly, walked heavily over to the table. She took out some paper, and her hand began moving rapidly over it. This is what she wrote in reply:

“My dear and excellent friend. Your letter of the thirteenth has given me great joy. So you still love me, my poetic Julie. Absence, of which you say so much evil, has therefore not had its usual effect on you. You complain of absence—what should I say, if I dared complain, deprived as I am of all those who are dear to me? Ah! if we did not have religion to console us, life would be very sad. Why do you suppose that I look sternly upon you when you speak to me of your affection for the young man? In that respect I am strict only with myself. I understand these feelings in others and, though I cannot approve of them, never having felt them, I do not condemn them. It merely seems to me that Christian love, love of one’s neighbor, love for one’s enemies, is more meritorious, sweeter, and more beautiful than are the feelings that the fine eyes of a young man can inspire in a poetic and loving young girl such as you.

“The news of Count Bezukhov’s death reached us before your letter, and my father was deeply affected by it. He says that the count was the penultimate representative of the great century and that now it is his turn, but that he will do all he can to make his turn come as late as possible. May God preserve us from this terrible misfortune! I cannot share your opinion of Pierre, whom I knew as a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I esteem most in people. As for his inheritance and the part Prince Vasili played in it, it is very sad for them both. Ah! dear friend, the words of our divine Savior, that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, are terribly true; I pity Prince Vasili, and I am even sorrier for Pierre. So young and burdened with such wealth—how many temptations he will have to undergo! If I were asked what I desired most in the world, it would be to be poorer than the poorest of beggars.

“A thousand thanks, dear friend, for the work you are sending me, which is so greatly in vogue among you. However, since you tell me that amid several good things there are others that the feeble human understanding cannot grasp, it seems to me rather pointless to occupy oneself with unintelligible reading, which for that very reason could bear no fruit. I have never been able to understand the passion certain people have for muddling their understanding by devoting themselves to mystical books, which merely raise doubts in their minds, excite their imagination, and give them a tendency toward exaggeration entirely contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us read the Apostles and the Gospel. Let us not seek to penetrate what mysteries they contain, for how could we, miserable sinners that we are, dare to claim initiation into the terrible and sacred secrets of Providence while we still bear this carnal covering, which raises an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us therefore confine ourselves to studying the sublime principles our divine Savior left us for our conduct here below; let us seek to conform to them and follow them; let us persuade ourselves that the less scope we give to our feeble human mind, the more pleasing it is to God, Who rejects all knowledge not proceeding from Him; that the less we seek to fathom what it has pleased Him to conceal from our knowledge, the sooner He will grant us its discovery through His divine spirit.”

“You treat me as though I were ill or a child. I see everything. Were you like this six months ago?”

“Lise, I ask you to stop,” Prince Andrei said even more emphatically.

Pierre, who had grown more and more agitated during this conversation, rose and went over to the princess. He seemed unable to bear the sight of tears and was himself ready to weep.

“Calm yourself, Princess. It only seems that way to you, because, I assure you, I have experienced it myself... why... because... No, forgive me, an outsider is out of place here... No, calm yourself... Farewell...”

Prince Andrei stopped him by the arm.

“No, stay, Pierre. The princess is so kind that she will not wish to deprive me of the pleasure of spending the evening with you.”

“No, he thinks only of himself,” the princess said, no longer restraining her angry tears.

“Lise,” Prince Andrei said drily, raising his voice to the pitch that indicates that patience is exhausted.

Suddenly the angry, squirrel-like expression on the princess’s pretty little face was replaced by an attractive, compassion-arousing expression of fear; she glanced up from under her brows at her husband with her beautiful little eyes, and there appeared on her face the timid and confessing expression seen in a dog rapidly but feebly wagging its lowered tail.

“My God, my God!” the princess said and, gathering up a fold of her dress with one hand, went over to her husband and kissed him on the forehead.

“Good night, Lise,” Prince Andrei said, rising and courteously kissing her hand as though she were a stranger.

The friends were silent. Neither one nor the other began to speak. Pierre kept glancing at Prince Andrei; Prince Andrei rubbed his forehead with his small hand.

“Let’s go to supper,” he said with a sigh, rising and making for the door.

They entered an elegant, newly and richly appointed dining room. Everything, from the napkins to the silver, faience, and crystal, bore that peculiar stamp of newness found in the household of a young married couple. In the middle of supper Prince Andrei leaned on his elbow and, like a man who has long had something on his mind and suddenly resolves to speak out, began talking with an expression of nervous irritation such as Pierre had never before seen in his friend:

“Never, never marry, my friend; that is my advice to you: do not marry until you can tell yourself that you have done everything you could, and until you have ceased to love the woman you have chosen, until you see her clearly; otherwise you will make a cruel and irreparable mistake. Marry when you are an old man, good for nothing... Otherwise everything good and lofty in you will be lost. It will all be frittered away on trifles. Yes, yes, yes! Don’t look at me with such astonishment. If you expect anything of yourself in the future, then at every step you will feel that for you everything is over, everything is closed off, except the drawing room, where you will stand on the same level as a court lackey and an idiot... Ah, what’s the use!”

He waved his hand energetically.

Pierre took off his spectacles, which changed his face and made its kindness still more apparent, and looked at his friend in astonishment.

“My wife,” Prince Andrei continued, “is an excellent woman. She is one of those rare women with whom a man can feel secure about his honor; but, my God, what would I not give now not to be married! I am telling you this alone, and you are the first person I have told, because I love you.”

As Prince Andrei said this, he looked even less than before like the Bolkonsky who had sat sprawled in Anna Pavlovna’s armchairs, narrowing his eyes and speaking French phrases through his teeth. His dry face quivered all over with the nervous animation of every muscle; his eyes, in which the fire of life had earlier seemed extinguished, now shone with a radiant, brilliant gleam. It was evident that the more lifeless he seemed at ordinary times, the more energetic he was in moments of irritation.

“You do not understand why I am saying this,” he continued. “Why, it is a whole life story. You speak of Bonaparte and his career,” he said, though Pierre had not spoken of Bonaparte. “You speak of Bonaparte; but Bonaparte, when he was working, went step by step toward his goal; he was free, he had nothing except his goal—and he attained it. But bind yourself to a woman, and, like a shackled convict, you lose all freedom. And all the hope and strength in you merely weigh you down and torment you with remorse. Drawing rooms, gossip, balls, vanity, triviality—that is the enchanted circle from which I cannot escape. I am now setting off for war, for the greatest war there has ever been, yet I know nothing and am good for nothing. I am very amiable and very caustic,” Prince Andrei continued, “and at Anna Pavlovna’s they listen to me. And this stupid society, without which my wife cannot live, and these women... If only you could know what all these distinguished women and women in general are like! My father is right. Selfishness, vanity, dull-wittedness, triviality in everything—that is what women are when they show themselves as they really are. You look at them in society and it seems there is something there, but there is nothing, nothing, nothing! Yes, do not marry, my dear soul, do not marry,” Prince Andrei concluded.

“It seems funny to me,” Pierre said, “that you consider yourself, yourself, incapable, and your life a ruined life. You have everything, everything ahead of you. And you...”

He did not say what “you” meant, but his tone already showed how highly he valued his friend and how much he expected of him in the future.

“How can he say that?” Pierre thought. Pierre regarded Prince Andrei as a model of every perfection precisely because Prince Andrei combined to the highest degree all those qualities that Pierre lacked and that could best be expressed by the concept of strength of will. Pierre was always amazed by Prince Andrei’s ability to deal calmly with all kinds of people, by his extraordinary memory and erudition—he read everything, knew everything, and had an understanding of everything—and, most of all, by his ability to work and study. If Pierre was often struck by Andrei’s lack of a capacity for dreamy philosophizing—to which Pierre was particularly inclined—he saw even this not as a defect but as a strength.

In the best, friendliest, and simplest relationships, flattery or praise is as necessary as grease is necessary for wheels if they are to turn.

“I am a finished man,” Prince Andrei said. “What is there to say about me? Let us talk about you,” he said after a pause, smiling at his consoling thoughts.

That smile was reflected on Pierre’s face at the same moment.

“And what is there to say about me?” Pierre said, spreading his mouth into a carefree, cheerful smile. “What am I? I am a bastard!” And he suddenly flushed crimson. It was evident that he had made a great effort to say this. “Without a name, without a fortune... And, really, what does it matter...” But he did not say what really did not matter. “I am free for now, and I am happy. I simply have no idea what I should begin to do. I wanted to consult you seriously.”

“You see,” the adjutant was saying, “it is a tangled story. This proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed. He ordered an investigation. So Gavrilo Ivanych made inquiries: this proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three pairs of hands. He would go to one man: ‘Whom did you get it from?’—‘So-and-so.’ He would go to that man: ‘Whom did you get it from?’ and so on, until they reached Vereshchagin... a half-educated young merchant, you know, a dear little merchant,” the adjutant said with a smile. “They ask him: ‘Whom did you get it from?’ And the main thing is that we know whom he got it from. He could have got it from no one but the postmaster. But there had evidently been some collusion between them. He says: ‘From no one; I wrote it myself.’ They threatened and entreated him, but he stood by it: ‘I wrote it myself.’ That was how it was reported to the count. The count ordered him to be summoned. ‘Whom did you get the proclamation from?’—‘I wrote it myself.’ Well, you know the count!” the adjutant said with a proud and cheerful smile. “He flew into a terrible rage, and just think of it: such insolence, lying, and obstinacy!...

“Ah! The count wanted him to implicate Klyucharev, I understand!” said Pierre.

“Not at all,” the adjutant said in alarm. “There were sins enough against Klyucharev even without that, and that is why he was exiled. But the point is that the count was extremely indignant. ‘How could you have written it?’ says the count. He took the Hamburg newspaper from the table. ‘Here it is. You did not write it; you translated it, and translated it badly at that, because, fool that you are, you do not even know French.’ Well, what do you think? ‘No,’ he says, ‘I have not read any newspapers; I wrote it myself.’—‘And if that is so, then you are a traitor, and I shall have you brought to trial, and you will be hanged.

“‘Tell me, whom did you receive it from?’—‘I have not seen any newspapers; I wrote it myself.’ And that is how the matter remained. The count summoned his father too, but he stood his ground. And they put him on trial and sentenced him, I think, to hard labor. Now his father has come to plead for him. But he is a worthless brat! You know the sort: a merchant’s little son, a fop and seducer, who attended some lectures somewhere and now thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That is the kind of fine fellow he is! His father has a tavern here by the Stone Bridge, and in the tavern, you know, there is a large icon of God Almighty, depicted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other; well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what do you think he did? He found a scoundrel of a painter...

XI.

In the middle of this new story, Pierre was summoned to the commander in chief.

Pierre entered Count Rastopchin’s study. Rastopchin was frowning and rubbing his forehead and eyes with his hand as Pierre entered. A short man was saying something and, as soon as Pierre came in, fell silent and left.

“Ah! Good day, great warrior,” said Rastopchin as soon as the man had left. “I have heard about your feats! But that is not the point. My dear fellow, between ourselves, are you a Freemason?” Count Rastopchin said in a stern tone, as though there were something bad in that, but something he intended to forgive. Pierre was silent. “My dear fellow, I am well informed, but I know that there are Masons and Masons, and I hope you do not belong to those who, under the guise of saving the human race, wish to destroy Russia.”

“Yes, I am a Freemason,” Pierre replied.

“Well then, you see, my dear fellow. I think you are not unaware that Messrs. Speransky and Magnitsky have been sent where they belong; the same has been done with Mr. Klyucharev, and likewise with others who, under the guise of building the temple of Solomon, sought to destroy the temple of their fatherland. You can understand that there are reasons for this and that I could not have exiled the local postmaster if he had not been a dangerous man. I now know that you sent him your carriage to take him out of the city and even that you accepted papers from him for safekeeping. I love you and wish you no harm, and since you are half my age, I advise you, as a father, to break off all relations with people of that sort and to leave here yourself as soon as possible.”

“But what is Klyucharev guilty of, Count?” Pierre asked.

“That is for me to know and not for you to ask me,” Rastopchin shouted.

“If he is accused of circulating Napoleon’s proclamations, that has not been proved,” said Pierre, without looking at Rastopchin, “and Vereshchagin...”

“There we are,” Rastopchin suddenly shouted, frowning, interrupting Pierre, and raising his voice even louder than before. “Vereshchagin is a traitor and a betrayer who will receive the punishment he deserves,” Rastopchin said with the heat of malice with which people speak when recalling an insult. “But I did not summon you to discuss my affairs, but to give you advice—or an order, if that is what you want. I ask you to break off relations with gentlemen such as Klyucharev and to leave this place. And I shall knock the foolishness out of anyone, whoever he may be.” And, probably realizing that he seemed to be shouting at Bezukhov, who had not yet been guilty of anything, he added, taking Pierre amicably by the hand: “We are on the eve of a public disaster, and I have no time to say pleasant things to everyone who has business with me. Sometimes my head is in a whirl! Well then, my dear fellow, what are you doing, you personally?”

“Why, nothing,” Pierre replied, still without raising his eyes or changing the thoughtful expression on his face.

The count frowned.

“A friend’s advice, my dear fellow. Clear out, and as soon as possible; that is all I have to say to you. A word to the wise is enough! Good-bye, my dear fellow. Oh, yes,” he called after him from the doorway, “is it true that the countess has fallen into the clutches of the holy fathers of the Society of Jesus?”

Pierre did not answer and, frowning and angry as no one had ever seen him, left Rastopchin.
