By the time he arrived home, dusk was already falling. About eight different people came to see him that evening: the committee secretary, the colonel of his battalion, his steward, his butler, and various petitioners. They all had matters requiring Pierre’s attention that he had to settle. Pierre understood nothing, took no interest in these matters, and gave only such answers to all their questions as would rid him of these people. At last, when he was alone, he unsealed and read his wife’s letter.

“They are soldiers at the battery, Prince Andrei has been killed... the old man... Simplicity is submission to God. One must suffer... the meaning of everything... one must unite... a wife is getting married... One must forget and understand...” And, going over to the bed without undressing, he flung himself down on it and immediately fell asleep.

When he awoke the next morning, the butler came to report that a police official specially sent by Count Rastopchin had come to find out whether Count Bezukhov had left or was leaving.

About ten different people who had business with Pierre were waiting for him in the drawing room. Pierre dressed hurriedly and, instead of going to those who were waiting for him, went to the back porch and left through the gate from there.

From then until the end of the devastation of Moscow, none of the Bezukhov household, despite all their searching, saw Pierre again or knew where he was.

After reading about the dangers threatening Russia, about the hopes placed by the sovereign in Moscow, and especially in its renowned nobility, Sonya, with a tremor in her voice arising chiefly from the attention with which she was being listened to, read the final words: “We shall not delay in coming personally into the midst of our people in this capital and in other places of our realm, to confer and to direct all our levies, both those now barring the enemy’s way and those newly raised to strike him down wherever he may appear. May the destruction into which he thinks to cast us recoil upon his own head, and may Europe, freed from bondage, magnify the name of Russia!”

“There, now! That’s the way!” cried the count, opening his moist eyes and pausing several times to snuffle, as though a bottle of strong vinegar salts were being held to his nose. “The sovereign need only say the word, and we shall sacrifice everything and begrudge nothing.”

Shinshin had not yet had time to make the joke he had prepared about the count’s patriotism when Natasha sprang up from her seat and ran over to her father.

“What a darling this papa is!” she said, kissing him, and she looked at Pierre again with that unconscious coquetry which had returned to her together with her animation.

“There’s a patriot for you!” said Shinshin.

“I’m not a patriot at all, but simply...” Natasha replied, offended. “Everything is a joke to you, but this is no joke at all...”

“What jokes!” the count repeated. “He need only say the word, and we shall all go... We’re not some sort of Germans...”

“But did you notice,” said Pierre, “that it says, ‘to confer’?”

“Well, whatever it may be for...”

At that moment Petya, to whom no one was paying any attention, went up to his father and, red all over, said in a breaking voice, now deep, now shrill:

“Well, now, Papa, I shall say it once and for all—and Mama too, as you please—I shall say it once and for all: you must let me enter military service, because I cannot... that is all...”

The countess raised her eyes to heaven in horror, threw up her hands, and turned angrily to her husband.

“There, that’s what your talk has led to!” she said.

But the count recovered from his emotion that very moment.

“Come, come,” he said. “Here’s another warrior! Stop this nonsense: you must study.”

“It is not nonsense, Papa. Fedya Obolensky is younger than I am and he is going too, and most importantly, it makes no difference, I cannot learn anything now, when...” Petya stopped, flushed until he broke into a sweat, and said after all, “when the fatherland is in danger.”

“That will do, that will do—nonsense...”

“But you yourself said that we would sacrifice everything.”

“Petya! I am telling you to be quiet,” shouted the count, glancing at his wife, who had gone pale and was staring fixedly at her younger son.

“And I am telling you. Pyotr Kirillovich will say so too...”

“I am telling you—it is rubbish; the milk is not yet dry on your lips, and you want to enter military service! Come, come, I am telling you,” and the count, taking the papers with him, probably to read them once more in his study before resting, left the room.

“Pyotr Kirillovich, well then, let us go and have a smoke...”

Pierre was in a state of confusion and indecision. Natasha’s unaccustomedly shining and animated eyes, constantly turning toward him with more than tenderness, had brought him into this state.

“No, I think I shall go home...”

“Home? But you meant to spend the evening with us... And you have begun coming so rarely as it is. And this girl of mine...” said the count good-naturedly, pointing to Natasha, “is cheerful only when you are here...”

“Yes, I had forgotten... I absolutely must go home... Business...” Pierre said hurriedly.

“Well then, good-bye,” said the count, finally leaving the room.

“Why are you leaving? Why are you upset? Why?...” Natasha asked Pierre, looking challengingly into his eyes.

“Because I love you!” he wanted to say, but he did not say it; he flushed to the point of tears and lowered his eyes.

“Because it is better for me to visit you less often... Because... no, I simply have business...”

“Why? No, tell me,” Natasha began resolutely, and suddenly fell silent. They both looked at each other in fear and confusion. He tried to smile, but could not: his smile expressed suffering, and he silently kissed her hand and went out.

Pierre resolved within himself not to visit the Rostovs anymore.

XXI.

After receiving this categorical refusal, Petya went to his room and there, having locked himself away from everyone, wept bitterly. Everyone behaved as though they had noticed nothing when he came to tea, silent and gloomy, with tear-stained eyes.

The next day the sovereign arrived. Several of the Rostovs’ household servants asked leave to go and see the Tsar. That morning Petya spent a long time dressing, combing his hair, and arranging his collars the way grown men did. He frowned at himself in the mirror, made gestures, shrugged his shoulders, and finally, without telling anyone, put on his forage cap and left the house by the back steps, trying not to be noticed. Petya had resolved to go straight to the place where the sovereign was and to explain directly to some chamberlain (Petya imagined that the sovereign was always surrounded by chamberlains) that he, Count Rostov, despite his youth, wished to serve the fatherland, that youth could be no obstacle to devotion, and that he was ready... While getting dressed, Petya had prepared many splendid words that he would say to the chamberlain.

Petya counted on the success of his presentation to the sovereign precisely because he was a child (Petya even thought how everyone would marvel at his youth), while at the same time, in the arrangement of his collars, in his hairstyle, and in his sedate, deliberate gait, he wanted to present himself as an old man. But the farther he walked, and the more he was distracted by the ever-growing crowds arriving at the Kremlin, the more he forgot to maintain the sedateness and deliberateness proper to grown men. As he approached the Kremlin, he began to concern himself with not being jostled and resolutely thrust out his elbows on either side with a menacing air. But at the Trinity Gate, despite all his resolution, people who probably did not know the patriotic purpose for which he was going to the Kremlin pressed him so hard against the wall that he had to submit and stop while carriages passed through the gate with a rumbling sound echoing beneath the arches. Beside Petya stood a peasant woman with a footman, two merchants, and a retired soldier. After standing in the gate for some time, Petya, without waiting for all the carriages to pass, wanted to move on before the others and began resolutely working with his elbows; but the woman standing opposite him, at whom he first directed his elbows, shouted at him angrily:

“Why are you pushing, young master? You can see everyone is standing still. Why must you shove your way through?”

“Then everyone will start shoving through,” said the footman, and, also beginning to work with his elbows, he squeezed Petya into a stinking corner of the gateway.

Petya wiped away with his hands the sweat covering his face and straightened his collars, which had gone limp with sweat and which he had arranged so well at home, the way grown men did.

Petya felt that he looked unpresentable and was afraid that if he appeared before the chamberlains in such a state, he would not be admitted to the sovereign. But there was no possibility of tidying himself up or moving to another place because of the crush. One of the generals passing by was an acquaintance of the Rostovs. Petya wanted to ask for his help, but considered that this would be contrary to courage. When all the carriages had passed, the crowd surged forward and swept Petya out into the square, which was completely filled with people. There were people not only in the square, but on the slopes, on the roofs—everywhere. No sooner had Petya found himself in the square than he distinctly heard the sounds of bells and the joyful murmur of the people filling the entire Kremlin.

“What happened, then?” he asked himself. “I killed my wife’s lover—yes, killed my wife’s lover. Yes, that happened. Why? How did I come to this?” “Because you married her,” answered the inner voice.

“But what am I guilty of?” he asked. “Of marrying her without loving her, of deceiving both yourself and her”—and he vividly pictured that moment after dinner at Prince Vasily’s when he had uttered those words that would not come from him: “I love you.” “It all came from that! Even then I felt,” he thought, “I felt then that it was not right, that I had no right to do it. And so it turned out.” He remembered the honeymoon and blushed at the recollection. Especially vivid, insulting, and shameful to him was the memory of how once, soon after his marriage, in the twelfth hour of the day, wearing a silk dressing gown, he had come from the bedroom into his study and there found the chief steward, who bowed respectfully, looked at Pierre’s face and at his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as though expressing with that smile respectful sympathy for his employer’s happiness.

“And how many times I was proud of her, proud of her majestic beauty, of her social tact,” he thought; “proud of that house of mine in which she received all Petersburg, proud of her unapproachability and beauty. So that is what I was proud of! At the time I thought I did not understand her. How often, when pondering her character, I told myself that I was to blame for not understanding her, for not understanding that perpetual calm, contentment, and absence of all passions and desires, while the whole answer lay in that terrible phrase: that she was a depraved woman. I told myself that terrible phrase, and everything became clear!

“Anatole used to go to her to borrow money from her and kiss her bare shoulders. She did not give him money, but she allowed him to kiss her. Her father, as a joke, tried to arouse her jealousy; with a calm smile she said she was not so stupid as to be jealous: let him do whatever he wants, she said of me. I once asked her whether she felt any signs of pregnancy. She laughed contemptuously and said that she was not a fool who wanted to have children, and that she would have no children by me.”

Then he remembered the coarseness and clarity of her thoughts and the vulgarity of the expressions characteristic of her, despite her upbringing in the highest aristocratic circle. “I’m not some sort of fool... go and try it yourself... go take a walk,” she would say. Often, looking at her success in the eyes of old and young men and women, Pierre could not understand why he did not love her. “Why, I never loved her,” Pierre told himself; “I knew she was a depraved woman,” he repeated to himself, but had not dared admit it.

“And now Dolokhov—there he is, sitting in the snow and forcing a smile, and perhaps dying, responding to my remorse with some sort of feigned bravado!”

Pierre was one of those people who, despite their outward, so-called weakness of character, do not seek a confidant for their grief. He worked through his grief alone within himself.

“She is to blame for everything, for everything—she alone,” he told himself; “but what of it? Why did I bind myself to her, why did I say to her, ‘I love you,’ which was a lie and worse than a lie?” he told himself. “I am guilty and must bear... What? The disgrace of my name, the unhappiness of my life? Ah, it is all nonsense,” he thought, “the disgrace of one’s name and honor—it is all conventional, all independent of me.

“Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal,” it occurred to Pierre, “and they were right from their point of view, just as those who died martyrs’ deaths for him and numbered him among the saints were also right. Then Robespierre was executed for being a despot. Who is right, who is guilty? No one. But you are alive, so live: tomorrow you will die, as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth suffering when one has only a second left to live in comparison with eternity?” But at the very moment when he considered himself calmed by reasoning of that kind, he would suddenly picture her in those moments when he had most strongly displayed his insincere love for her, and he would feel a rush of blood to his heart and have to get up again, move about, and break and tear whatever came to hand. “Why did I say to her, ‘I love you’?” he kept repeating to himself. And after repeating that question for the tenth time, Molière’s line occurred to him: “But what the devil was he doing in that galley?” and he laughed at himself.

At night he summoned his valet and ordered him to pack for the journey to Petersburg. He could not remain under the same roof with her. He could not imagine how he would speak to her now. He decided that the next day he would leave and leave her a letter in which he would announce his intention of separating from her forever.

In the morning, when the valet entered the study carrying coffee, Pierre was lying on the ottoman, asleep with an open book in his hand.

He woke and for a long time looked around in fright, unable to understand where he was.

“The Countess ordered me to ask whether Your Excellency is at home,” said the valet.

But before Pierre had time to decide on the answer he would give, the Countess herself entered the room, calmly and majestically, wearing a white satin dressing gown embroidered in silver and with her hair simply arranged—two enormous braids, in the form of a diadem, encircled her lovely head twice; only on her marble, slightly prominent forehead was a crease of anger. With her imperturbable composure, she did not begin speaking in the valet’s presence. She knew about the duel and had come to speak about it. She waited until the valet had set out the coffee and left. Pierre looked timidly at her through his spectacles, and, as a hare surrounded by dogs, flattening its ears, continues to lie in sight of its enemies, so he tried to continue reading; but he felt that this was senseless and impossible and again glanced timidly at her. She did not sit down, but looked at him with a contemptuous smile, waiting for the valet to leave.

“What is this now? What have you done, I ask you?” she said sternly.

“Me? What have I done?” said Pierre.

“So, a brave man has turned up! Well, answer me: what was this duel about? What did you mean to prove by it? What? I ask you.” Pierre turned heavily on the sofa, opened his mouth, but could not answer.

“If you will not answer, then I shall tell you...” Hélène continued. “You believe everything you are told. You were told...” Hélène laughed, “that Dolokhov is my lover,” she said in French, with her coarse precision of speech, pronouncing the word “lover” like any other word, “and you believed it! But what did you prove by it? What did you prove by this duel? That you are a fool, that you are an idiot—everyone knew that already! Where will this lead? To my becoming the laughingstock of all Moscow; to everyone saying that, while drunk and not knowing what you were doing, you challenged a man of whom you are jealous without any grounds”—Hélène raised her voice more and more and grew animated—“who is better than you in every respect...”}

Natasha did not remember how that day passed, or the night, or the next day and the next night. She did not sleep and did not leave her mother’s side. Natasha’s love, steadfast and patient, not as an explanation, not as consolation, but as a summons to life, seemed every second to embrace the countess from all sides. On the third night the countess grew quiet for several minutes, and Natasha closed her eyes, resting her head on the arm of the chair. The bed creaked; Natasha opened her eyes. The countess was sitting up in bed and speaking softly.

“How glad I am that you have come. You are tired; would you like some tea?” Natasha went over to her. “You have grown more handsome and manly,” the countess continued, taking her daughter by the hand.

“Mamma, what are you saying!…”

“Natasha, he is gone, gone forever!” And, embracing her daughter, the countess began to weep for the first time.

III.

Princess Marya postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha’s place, but they could not. They saw that she alone could keep her mother from mad despair. For three weeks Natasha remained constantly at her mother’s side, slept in an armchair in her room, gave her drink and food, and talked to her without ceasing—talked because her tender, caressing voice alone soothed the countess.

The mother’s spiritual wound could not heal. Petya’s death had torn away half her life. A month after the news of Petya’s death, which had found her a fresh and vigorous woman of fifty, she emerged from her room half dead and taking no part in life—an old woman. But the same wound that had half killed the countess, this new wound, called Natasha back to life.

A spiritual wound caused by the rending of a spiritual being, strange though it may seem, closes little by little, just like a physical wound. And after a deep wound has healed and its edges seem to have come together, a spiritual wound, like a physical one, heals only through the force of life pushing outward from within.

Natasha’s wound healed in the same way. She thought that her life was over. But suddenly her love for her mother showed her that the essence of her life—love—was still alive within her. Love awoke, and life awoke.

Prince Andrei’s last days had bound Natasha to Princess Marya. The new misfortune brought them still closer together. Princess Marya postponed her departure and, for the last three weeks, tended Natasha as though she were a sick child. The final weeks Natasha had spent in her mother’s room had undermined her physical strength.

One day in the middle of the day, Princess Marya, noticing that Natasha was trembling with a feverish chill, took her to her own room and put her to bed. Natasha lay down, but when Princess Marya, after lowering the blinds, was about to leave, Natasha called her over.

“I do not want to sleep. Marie, sit with me.”

“You are tired—try to fall asleep.”

“No, no. Why did you take me away? She will ask for me.”

“She is much better. She spoke so well today,” said Princess Marya.

Natasha lay in bed and, in the room’s half-darkness, studied Princess Marya’s face.

“Does she look like him?” Natasha thought. “Yes, she does and she does not. But she is special, a stranger, entirely new, unknown. And she loves me. What is in her soul? Everything good. But how? How does she think? How does she look at me? Yes, she is beautiful.”

“Masha,” she said, timidly drawing her hand toward her. “Masha, do not think that I am bad. No? Masha, darling. How I love you. Let us be completely, completely friends.”

And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing Princess Marya’s hands and face. Princess Marya was embarrassed and delighted by this expression of Natasha’s feelings.

From that day onward, there arose between Princess Marya and Natasha that passionate and tender friendship which exists only between women. They kissed constantly, said tender words to each other, and spent most of their time together. If one went out, the other became anxious and hurried to join her. Together they felt greater harmony with each other than they did apart, each alone with herself. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them: it was the exclusive feeling that life was possible only in each other’s presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours at a time; sometimes, already lying in their beds, they began to talk and talked until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Marya told of her childhood, of her mother, of her father, of her dreams; and Natasha, who before had turned away with calm incomprehension from this life of devotion and submission, from the poetry of Christian self-renunciation, now, feeling herself bound to Princess Marya by love, came to love Princess Marya’s past as well and understood the aspect of life that had previously been incomprehensible to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-renunciation to her own life, because she was accustomed to seeking other joys, but she understood and came to love in another this virtue that had previously been incomprehensible to her. For Princess Marya, who listened to stories of Natasha’s childhood and early youth, a previously incomprehensible aspect of life was likewise revealed: faith in life, in the pleasures of life.

Still, just as before, they did not speak of him, so as not to disturb with words what seemed to them the loftiness of the feeling within them; and this silence about him caused them, little by little and without believing it, to forget him.

Natasha grew thin and pale and became so physically weak that everyone constantly spoke about her health, and this pleased her. But sometimes she was unexpectedly seized not only by fear of death, but by fear of illness, weakness, and loss of beauty; and at times she involuntarily examined her bare arm attentively, amazed at its thinness, or in the mornings stared in the mirror at her elongated, pitiful face, as it seemed to her. It seemed to her that this was how it had to be, and at the same time she grew frightened and sad.

Once she went upstairs quickly and became heavily out of breath. At once, involuntarily, she invented an errand for herself downstairs, and from there ran upstairs again, testing her strength and observing herself.

Another time she called Dunyasha, and her voice quavered. She called her once more, even though she could hear her footsteps—called in that full, deep voice in which she used to sing, and listened to it.

She did not know it and would not have believed it, but beneath the layer of silt that seemed to her impenetrable and had covered her soul, slender, tender young blades of grass were already pushing through; they were destined to take root and so cover with their living shoots the grief that had crushed her that it would soon be neither visible nor noticeable. The wound was healing from within.

At the end of January Princess Marya left for Moscow, and the count insisted that Natasha go with her in order to consult the doctors.

“How am I to understand it!” her father cried angrily. “Prince Vasili finds you to his taste as a daughter-in-law and makes you a proposal on behalf of his ward. That is how you are to understand it. ‘How am I to understand it?!’... And I am asking you.”

“I do not know what you think, Father,” the princess said in a whisper.

“I? I? What have I to do with it? Leave me out of it. I am not the one who is going to marry. What do you think? That is what I should like to know.”

The princess saw that her father regarded the matter unfavorably, but at that very moment the thought came to her that now or never the fate of her life would be decided. She lowered her eyes so as not to see the gaze under whose influence she felt that she could not think, but could only obey out of habit, and said:

“I desire only one thing—to carry out your will,” she said, “but if my own desire had to be expressed...”

She did not have time to finish. The prince interrupted her.

“And splendid!” he shouted. “He will take you with your dowry, and pick up Mlle Bourienne into the bargain. She will be the wife, and you...”

The prince stopped. He noticed the effect these words had produced on his daughter. She lowered her head and was about to cry.

“Come, come, I am joking, I am joking,” he said. “Remember one thing, Princess: I adhere to the rule that a maiden has a perfect right to choose. And I give you freedom. Remember one thing: the happiness of your life depends on your decision. There is no need to speak of me.”

“But I do not know... Father.”

“There is no need to speak! He is ordered to; he will marry not only you, but anyone they please; while you are free to choose... Go to your room, think it over, and in an hour come to me and say in his presence: yes or no.

“I know you will pray. Well, pray if you like. Only it would be better to think. Go.”

“Yes or no, yes or no, yes or no!” he was still shouting as the princess, as though in a fog, already staggered out of the study.

Her fate was decided, and decided happily. But what her father had said about Mlle Bourienne—that insinuation was terrible. Granted, it was not true, but still it was terrible; she could not help thinking about it. She was walking straight ahead through the conservatory, seeing and hearing nothing, when suddenly Mlle Bourienne’s familiar whisper roused her. She raised her eyes and, two paces away, saw Anatole embracing the Frenchwoman and whispering something to her. With a terrible expression on his handsome face, Anatole looked round at Princess Marya and, during the first instant, did not release the waist of Mlle Bourienne, who had not seen her.

“Who is there? Why? Wait!” Anatole’s face seemed to say. Princess Marya looked at them in silence. She could not understand it. At last Mlle Bourienne gave a cry and ran away. With a cheerful smile, Anatole bowed to Princess Marya, as though inviting her to laugh at this strange incident, and, shrugging his shoulders, went through the door leading to his quarters.

An hour later Tikhon came to summon Princess Marya. He summoned her to the prince and added that Prince Vasili Sergeyevich was there as well. When Tikhon came, the princess was sitting on the sofa in her room, holding the weeping Mlle Bourienne in her arms. Princess Marya was gently stroking her head. The princess’s beautiful eyes, with all their former serenity and radiance, looked with tender love and pity at Mlle Bourienne’s pretty little face.

“No, Princess, I am lost forever in your heart,” said Mlle Bourienne.

“Why? I love you more than ever,” said Princess Marya, “and I shall try to do everything in my power for your happiness.”

“But you despise me; you, who are so pure, will never understand this aberration of passion. Ah, it is only my poor mother...”

“I understand everything,” Princess Marya replied with a sad smile. “Calm yourself, my friend. I shall go to my father,” she said, and went out.

Prince Vasili, with one leg crossed high and a snuffbox in his hands, looking as though he were moved beyond measure, as though he himself both pitied and laughed at his own sensitivity, was sitting with a smile of tender emotion on his face when Princess Marya entered. He hastily raised a pinch of snuff to his nose.

“Ah, my dear, my dear,” he said, rising and taking her by both hands. He sighed and added, “My son’s fate is in your hands. Decide, my dear, my darling, my sweet Marie, whom I have always loved as my own daughter.”

He stepped away. A genuine tear appeared in his eyes.

“Frr... frr...” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich snorted.

“The prince, on behalf of his ward... his son, is making you a proposal. Do you or do you not wish to be the wife of Prince Anatole Kuragin? You say yes or no!” he shouted. “And afterward I reserve the right to state my own opinion as well. Yes, my opinion, and only my own opinion,” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich added, turning to Prince Vasili and responding to his imploring expression. “Yes or no?”

“My desire, Father, is never to leave you, never to separate my life from yours. I do not wish to marry,” she said resolutely, looking with her beautiful eyes at Prince Vasili and at her father.

“Nonsense, foolishness! Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich shouted with a frown. He took his daughter by the hand, bent her toward him, and did not kiss her, but merely bent his forehead to hers and touched her; and he squeezed the hand he was holding so hard that she winced and cried out.

Prince Vasili rose.

“My dear, I shall tell you that this is a moment I shall never, never forget; but, my dear, will you not give us a little hope of moving this heart, so kind, so generous? Say that perhaps... The future is so vast. Say: perhaps.”

“Prince, what I have said is all that is in my heart. I thank you for the honor, but I shall never be your son’s wife.”

“Well, that is settled, my dear fellow. Very glad to see you, very glad to see you. Go to your room, Princess, go,” said the old prince. “Very, very glad to see you,” he repeated, embracing Prince Vasili.

“My calling is a different one,” Princess Marya thought to herself. “My calling is to be happy with another kind of happiness, the happiness of love and self-sacrifice. And whatever it may cost me, I shall make poor Amélie happy. She loves him so passionately. She repents so passionately. I shall do everything to arrange her marriage to him. If he is not rich, I shall give her the means; I shall ask Father, I shall ask Andrei. I shall be so happy when she is his wife. She is so unhappy, a stranger, alone, without help! And, my God, how passionately she loves him, if she could so forget herself. Perhaps I would have done the same!...” thought Princess Marya.

“Yes, love,” he thought again with perfect clarity, “but not the love that loves for something, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love that I experienced for the first time when, as I lay dying, I saw my enemy and loved him all the same. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and which needs no object. Even now I experience this blissful feeling. To love one’s neighbors, to love one’s enemies. To love everything—to love God in all His manifestations. One can love a dear person with human love; but only an enemy can be loved with divine love. And that was why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?... Loving with human love, one can pass from love to hatred; but divine love cannot change. Nothing, not death, nothing can destroy it. It is the essence of the soul. And how many people I have hated in my life. And of all people, I have loved and hated no one more than her.” And he vividly pictured Natasha, not as he had pictured her before, with only her charm, which gave him joy; but for the first time he pictured her soul. And he understood her feelings, her sufferings, her shame, her remorse. Now, for the first time, he understood the full cruelty of his refusal, saw the cruelty of his breaking with her. “If only it were possible for me to see her just once more. Once, looking into those eyes, to say...”

And piti-piti-piti and ti-ti, and piti-piti—boom, the fly struck against something... And his attention was suddenly transported into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something extraordinary was taking place. In that world, just as before, the whole edifice kept rising without collapsing; something kept stretching in the same way, the candle with its red circle burned in the same way, the same sphinx-shirt lay by the door; but in addition to all this, something creaked, a breath of fresh wind blew in, and a new white sphinx, standing upright, appeared before the door. And in the head of this sphinx were the pale face and shining eyes of that very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

“Oh, how oppressive this unceasing delirium is!” thought Prince Andrei, trying to banish that face from his imagination. But the face stood before him with the force of reality, and the face drew nearer. Prince Andrei wanted to return to the former world of pure thought, but he could not, and the delirium drew him into its realm. The quiet, whispering voice continued its measured babble, something pressed, something stretched, and the strange face stood before him.

Prince Andrei gathered all his strength to come to his senses; he stirred, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, his eyes grew dim, and, like a man plunging into water, he lost consciousness. When he came to, Natasha—the real, living Natasha whom, of all the people in the world, he most wished to love with that new, pure, divine love which had now been revealed to him—was kneeling before him. He understood that this was the living, real Natasha, and was not surprised, but quietly rejoiced. Natasha, on her knees, looked at him fearfully but intently (she could not move), holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and motionless. Only in its lower part did something tremble.

Prince Andrei sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.

“You?” he said. “How fortunate!”

With a swift but careful movement, Natasha moved closer to him on her knees and, taking his hand carefully, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.

“Forgive me!” she said in a whisper, raising her head and looking at him. “Forgive me!”

“I love you,” said Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me...”

“What is there to forgive?” asked Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me for what I d-did,” Natasha said in a barely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more rapidly, barely touching it with her lips.

“I love you more, better than before,” said Prince Andrei, raising her face with his hand so that he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, brimming with happy tears, looked at him timidly, compassionately, and with joyful love. Natasha’s thin, pale face with its swollen lips was more than plain; it was frightening. But Prince Andrei did not see that face; he saw the radiant eyes, which were beautiful. Voices were heard behind them.

Pyotr the valet, now fully awake, roused the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything that was happening and, carefully covering his unclothed body with a sheet, huddled on the bench.

“What is this?” said the doctor, raising himself from his bed. “Please leave, madam.”

At the same moment, a girl sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter was missing, was knocking at the door.

Like a somnambulist awakened in the middle of her sleep, Natasha left the room and, returning to her hut, fell sobbing onto her bed.

From that day onward, throughout the rest of the Rostovs’ journey, at every rest stop and overnight lodging, Natasha did not leave the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected either such fortitude or such skill in tending a wounded man from the young lady.

However dreadful the thought seemed to the countess that Prince Andrei might—very probably, according to the doctor—die on the journey in her daughter’s arms, she could not oppose Natasha. Although, as a result of the closeness now established between the wounded Prince Andrei and Natasha, it occurred to them that, should he recover, their former relationship as betrothed bridegroom and bride would be resumed, no one, least of all Natasha and Prince Andrei, spoke of it: the unresolved, looming question of life or death, not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, overshadowed every other supposition.

XXXIII.

Pierre awoke late on September 3. His head ached, the clothes in which he had slept without undressing weighed heavily on his body, and in his soul there was a vague awareness of something shameful committed the day before; that shameful thing was yesterday’s conversation with Captain Ramballe.

The clock showed eleven, but outside it seemed particularly overcast. Pierre rose, rubbed his eyes, and, seeing the pistol with the carved stock that Gerasim had put back on the writing desk, Pierre remembered where he was and what awaited him on that very day.

“Can I already be too late?” thought Pierre. “No, he will probably not make his entry into Moscow before twelve.” Pierre did not allow himself to reflect on what awaited him, but hastened to act as soon as possible.

After straightening his clothes, Pierre took the pistol in his hands and was already preparing to leave. But then, for the first time, it occurred to him how he was to carry this weapon—not in his hand, surely—through the streets. Even beneath his wide kaftan, it was difficult to conceal the large pistol. It could not be placed unnoticed either behind his belt or under his arm. Besides, the pistol was unloaded, and Pierre had not had time to load it. “The dagger will do just as well,” Pierre told himself, although more than once, while considering how to carry out his intention, he had concluded that the chief mistake of the student in 1809 had been that he had wanted to kill Napoleon with a dagger. But as though Pierre’s principal aim were not to carry out the deed he had conceived, but to show himself that he was not renouncing his intention and was doing everything to carry it out, Pierre hurriedly took the blunt, notched dagger in a green sheath which he had bought near the Sukharev Tower together with the pistol, and hid it under his waistcoat.

Princess Mary had long since put down her book: she sat silently, fixing her radiant eyes on the nurse’s wrinkled face, familiar to her down to its smallest details: on the lock of gray hair that had escaped from beneath her headscarf, on the hanging pouch of skin beneath her chin.

Nurse Savishna, with a stocking in her hands, was recounting in a quiet voice, without herself hearing or understanding her own words, the story she had told hundreds of times of how the late princess had given birth to Princess Mary in Kishinev, with a Moldavian peasant woman instead of a midwife.

“God will have mercy; doctors are never needed,” she was saying. Suddenly a gust of wind pressed against one of the room’s removable window frames (by the prince’s orders, one frame in every room was always taken out when the larks returned) and, knocking back the poorly fastened latch, set the damask curtain flapping and, blowing in cold and snow, extinguished the candle. Princess Mary shuddered; the nurse put down the stocking, went over to the window, leaned out, and began trying to catch the frame that had swung open. The cold wind fluttered the ends of her headscarf and the escaped gray locks of her hair.

“Princess, dearie, someone’s coming along the avenue!” she said, holding the frame without closing it. “With lanterns; it must be the doctor...”

“Oh, my God! Thank God!” said Princess Mary. “I must go and meet him: he does not know Russian.”

Princess Mary threw on a shawl and ran to meet the arrivals. As she passed through the anteroom, she saw through the window that some carriage and lanterns were standing at the entrance. She went out onto the stairs. A tallow candle stood on the newel post, running in the wind. The footman Philip, with a frightened face and another candle in his hand, stood lower down, on the first landing. Lower still, around the turn in the stairs, approaching footsteps in warm boots could be heard. And a voice that seemed familiar to Princess Mary was saying something.

“Thank God!” said the voice. “And Father?”

“He has retired for the night,” answered the voice of the steward Demyan, who was already downstairs.

Then the voice said something else, Demyan answered something, and the footsteps in warm boots began approaching more quickly around the unseen turn of the staircase. “It is Andrei!” thought Princess Mary. “No, it cannot be; it would be too extraordinary,” she thought, and at the very moment she was thinking this, the face and figure of Prince Andrei, wearing a fur coat with a collar sprinkled with snow, appeared on the landing where the footman stood with the candle. Yes, it was he, but pale and thin, with a changed expression on his face, strangely softened yet anxious. He came up the stairs and embraced his sister.

“You did not receive my letter?” he asked; and without waiting for an answer—which he would not have received in any case, because the princess could not speak—he turned back, and then, with the obstetrician who had come in after him (he had met up with him at the last posting station), he again mounted the stairs with quick steps and again embraced his sister.

“What a stroke of fate!” he said. “Dear Masha!” And, taking off his fur coat and boots, he went to the princess’s apartments.

IX.

The little princess lay on the pillows in a white cap. (Her pains had only just subsided.) Strands of black hair curled beside her inflamed, perspiring cheeks; her lovely little rosy mouth, with its upper lip covered in tiny black hairs, was open, and she smiled joyfully. Prince Andrei entered the room and stopped before her at the foot of the sofa on which she lay. Her shining eyes, gazing with childlike fear and agitation, came to rest on him without changing their expression. “I love all of you; I have done no harm to anyone; why am I suffering? Help me,” her expression said. She saw her husband but did not understand the significance of his appearing before her now. Prince Andrei walked around the sofa and kissed her on the forehead.

“My darling,” he said—a phrase he had never used to her. “God is merciful...” She looked at him questioningly, with childlike reproach.

“I expected help from you, and there is none, none—and you too!” her eyes said. She was not surprised that he had come; she did not understand that he had come. His arrival had no connection at all with her suffering or with relieving it. The agonies began again, and Marya Bogdanovna advised Prince Andrei to leave the room.

The obstetrician entered the room. Prince Andrei went out and, meeting Princess Mary, approached her again. They began speaking in whispers, but every moment their conversation fell silent. They waited and listened.

“Go, my friend,” said Princess Mary. Prince Andrei went back toward his wife and sat down in the adjoining room to wait. A woman came out of her room with a frightened face and became confused on seeing Prince Andrei. He covered his face with his hands and sat that way for several minutes. Pitiful, helplessly animal moans could be heard from behind the door. Prince Andrei stood up, went to the door, and tried to open it. Someone was holding the door shut.

“No, no, you cannot!” said a frightened voice from inside. He began pacing the room. The screams ceased; several more seconds passed. Suddenly a terrible scream—not her scream, she could not have screamed like that—rang out in the adjoining room. Prince Andrei ran to the door; the scream ceased, and the cry of a baby was heard.

“Why have they brought a baby in there?” Prince Andrei thought in the first instant. “A baby? What baby?... Why is there a baby in there? Or has a baby been born?”

When he suddenly understood the full joyful meaning of that cry, tears choked him, and, leaning both hands on the windowsill, he sobbed and wept as children weep. The door opened. The doctor, with his shirtsleeves rolled up, without his frock coat, pale and with a trembling jaw, came out of the room. Prince Andrei turned to him, but the doctor looked at him in bewilderment and, without saying a word, passed by. The woman ran out and, on seeing Prince Andrei, faltered on the threshold. He entered his wife’s room. She lay dead in the same position in which he had seen her five minutes before, and the same expression, despite the motionless eyes and the pallor of the cheeks, remained on that lovely, childlike little face with its upper lip covered in tiny black hairs.

“I love all of you and have done nothing bad to anyone, and what have you done to me?” said her lovely, pitiful, dead face. In the corner of the room, something small and red grunted and squeaked in Marya Bogdanovna’s trembling white hands.

Two hours later Prince Andrei entered his father’s study with quiet steps. The old man already knew everything. He was standing right by the door, and as soon as it opened, the old man silently clasped his son’s neck with his aged, hard hands, like a vise, and sobbed like a child.

Three days later the funeral service was held for the little princess, and, taking leave of her, Prince Andrei mounted the steps beside the coffin. And in the coffin was the same face, though the eyes were closed. “Oh, what have you done to me?” it still said, and Prince Andrei felt that something had been torn away in his soul, that he was guilty of a wrong he could neither make right nor forget. He could not weep. The old man also went up and kissed her waxen little hand, which lay calmly and loftily upon the other, and to him her face said: “Oh, what have you done to me, and why?” And the old man turned away angrily when he saw that face.

“If there is a God and there is a future life, then there is truth, there is virtue; and man’s highest happiness consists in striving to attain them. One must live, one must love, one must believe,” Pierre was saying, “that we do not live only now on this patch of earth, but that we have lived and shall live eternally there, in the whole of it” (he pointed to the sky). Prince Andrei stood leaning on the railing of the ferry and, as he listened to Pierre, gazed, without taking his eyes from it, at the red reflection of the sun on the water, which was turning blue. Pierre fell silent. It was completely quiet. The ferry had long since reached the bank, and only the waves of the current struck the bottom of the ferry with a faint sound. It seemed to Prince Andrei that this lapping of the waves added a refrain to Pierre’s words: “It is true; believe it.”

Prince Andrei sighed and looked with a radiant, childlike, tender gaze into Pierre’s flushed, ecstatic, yet still timid face—the face of a friend who held the leading place.

“Yes, if only it were so!” he said. “But let us go and sit down,” Prince Andrei added, and as he left the ferry, he looked at the sky to which Pierre had pointed, and for the first time since Austerlitz he saw that lofty, eternal sky which he had seen while lying on the field at Austerlitz; and something long dormant, something better that was within him, suddenly awoke joyfully and youthfully in his soul. This feeling vanished as soon as Prince Andrei once more entered the customary conditions of life, but he knew that this feeling, which he did not know how to develop, lived within him. His meeting with Pierre marked an epoch for Prince Andrei from which began a new life for him—outwardly the same as before, but new in his inner world.

XIII.

It was already growing dark when Prince Andrei and Pierre drove up to the main entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrei smilingly drew Pierre’s attention to the commotion that had arisen by the back porch. A bent old woman with a bundle on her back and a short man in a black garment, with long hair, saw the carriage driving in and rushed back toward the gate. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing back at the carriage, ran in fright onto the back porch.

“Those are Masha’s people of God,” said Prince Andrei. “They mistook us for Father. And this is the one thing in which she disobeys him: he orders these wanderers to be driven away, while she receives them.”

“But what are people of God?” Pierre asked.

Prince Andrei had no time to answer him. The servants came out to meet them, and he questioned them about where the old prince was and whether he was expected soon.

The old prince was still in town, and they expected him at any moment.

Prince Andrei took Pierre to his own suite of rooms, which was always kept in perfect order awaiting him in his father’s house, and went himself to the nursery.

“Let us go to my sister,” Prince Andrei said when he returned to Pierre. “I have not seen her yet; she is hiding now and sitting with her people of God. It serves her right: she will be embarrassed, and you will see the people of God. It is curious, upon my word.”

“What are people of God?” Pierre asked.

“You shall see.”

Princess Marya was indeed embarrassed and flushed in patches when they entered her room. In her cozy room, with icon lamps before the icon cases, a young boy with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk’s cassock, sat beside her on the sofa behind the samovar.

Nearby, in an armchair, sat a wrinkled, thin old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.

“André, why did you not warn me?” she said with gentle reproach, placing herself before her wanderers like a mother hen before her chicks.

“Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you,” she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrei, his friendship with Andrei’s wife, and, above all, his kind, simple face disposed her favorably toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes and seemed to say, “I love you very much, but please do not laugh at my people.” After exchanging their first words of greeting, they sat down.

“Ah, so Ivanushka is here too,” said Prince Andrei, pointing with a smile to the young wanderer.

“André!” Princess Marya said imploringly.

“You must know that she is a woman,” Andrei said to Pierre.

“André, in God’s name!” Princess Marya repeated.

It was evident that Prince Andrei’s mocking attitude toward the wanderers and Princess Marya’s futile defense of them were customary, established relations between them.

“But, my dear friend,” said Prince Andrei, “you ought, on the contrary, to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man.”

“Really?” Pierre said curiously and seriously—which made Princess Marya particularly grateful to him—peering through his spectacles into the face of Ivanushka, who, realizing that they were speaking about him, looked around at everyone with sly eyes.

Princess Marya was embarrassed for her people quite needlessly. They were not at all timid. The old woman, with her eyes lowered but glancing sidelong at those who had entered, had turned her cup upside down on its saucer and placed a bitten piece of sugar beside it; she sat calmly and motionlessly in her armchair, waiting to be offered more tea. Ivanushka, sipping from his saucer, looked at the young men from under his brows with sly, feminine eyes.

“Where were you—in Kiev?” Prince Andrei asked the old woman.

“I was, Father,” the talkative old woman replied. “At Christmas itself I was vouchsafed, at the saints’ shrines, to partake of the holy, heavenly mysteries. And now I come from Kolyazin, Father; a great grace has been revealed there...”

“And is Ivanushka with you?”

“I travel on my own, provider,” Ivanushka said, trying to speak in a bass voice. “It was only in Yukhnov that Pelageyushka and I met...”

Pelageyushka interrupted her companion; she evidently wanted to tell what she had seen.

“In Kolyazin, Father, a great grace has been revealed.”

“What, some new relics?” Prince Andrei asked.

“That is enough, Andrei,” said Princess Marya. “Do not tell it, Pelageyushka.”

“No... what are you saying, Mother? Why should I not tell it? I love him. He is kind. He is chosen by God; he, my benefactor, gave me ten rubles—I remember. When I was in Kiev, Kiryusha, the holy fool—a true man of God, who goes barefoot winter and summer—says to me: ‘Why do you go where you ought not? Go to Kolyazin; a miracle-working icon has been revealed there, the most holy Mother of God.’ At those words I bade farewell to the saints and set out...”

Everyone was silent; the wanderer alone spoke in a measured voice, drawing in her breath.

“I arrived, my dear father, and the people say to me: ‘A great grace has been revealed; holy oil is dripping from the cheek of the most holy Mother of God...’”

“Very well, very well, you can tell it later,” Princess Marya said, blushing.

“Allow me to ask her,” said Pierre. “Did you see it yourself?” he asked.

“Of course, Father, I was vouchsafed to see it myself. There was such a radiance upon the countenance, like the light of heaven, and from the Mother’s cheek it kept dripping and dripping...”

“But that is a deception,” Pierre said ingenuously, having listened attentively to the wanderer.

“Oh, Father, what are you saying!” Pelageyushka said in horror, turning to Princess Marya for protection.

“They are deceiving the people,” he repeated.

It kept seeming to her that at any moment now she would understand, would penetrate that toward which her soul’s gaze was directed with a terrible question beyond her strength.

At the end of December, in a black woolen dress, her braid carelessly tied in a knot, thin and pale, Natasha sat with her feet tucked under her in a corner of the sofa, tensely crumpling and releasing the ends of her sash, and looked at the corner of the door.

She looked toward where he had gone, to that other side of life. And that side of life, of which she had never thought before, which had previously seemed so distant and incredible to her, was now closer and dearer to her, more comprehensible, than this side of life, in which everything was either emptiness and destruction, or suffering and insult.

She looked toward where she knew he was; but she could not see him otherwise than as he had been here. She saw him again just as he had been in Mytishchi, at Troitsa, in Yaroslavl.

She saw his face, heard his voice, and repeated his words and her own words spoken to him, and sometimes invented for herself and for him new words that might have been spoken then.

There he lies in an armchair in his little velvet coat, his head propped on his thin, pale hand. His chest is terribly sunken and his shoulders are raised. His lips are firmly compressed, his eyes gleam, and a wrinkle springs up and vanishes on his pale forehead. One of his legs is trembling rapidly, almost imperceptibly. Natasha knows that he is struggling with excruciating pain. “What is this pain? Why pain? What does he feel? How does it hurt him?” Natasha thinks. He noticed her attention, raised his eyes, and, without smiling, began to speak.

“One thing is terrible,” he said. “It is to bind oneself forever to a suffering person. It is eternal torment.” And he looked at her searchingly. Natasha, as always, answered then before she had had time to think about what she was answering; she said, “It cannot go on like this, it will not; you will get well—completely.”

She now saw him again and now relived everything she had felt then. She remembered his long, sad, stern look at these words and understood the meaning of reproach and despair in that prolonged look.

“I agreed,” Natasha now said to herself, “that it would be terrible if he were always to remain suffering. I said it then only because it would have been terrible for him, but he understood it differently. He thought it would have been terrible for me. Even then he still wanted to live—he was afraid of death. And I said it to him so coarsely, so stupidly. I did not think that. I thought something entirely different. If I had said what I thought, I would have said: even if he were dying, were dying all the time before my eyes, I would have been happy compared with what I am now. Now... There is nothing, no one. Did he know that? No. He did not know and never will know. And now it can never, never be put right.” And again he spoke the same words to her, but now, in her imagination, Natasha answered him differently. She stopped him and said, “Terrible for you, but not for me. You must know that without you there is nothing for me in life, and to suffer with you is the greatest happiness for me.” And he took her hand and pressed it as he had pressed it on that terrible evening, four days before his death. And in her imagination she spoke to him still other tender, loving words that she might have spoken then. “I love you... you... I love you, I love you...” she said, convulsively clasping her hands and clenching her teeth with fierce effort.

And sweet grief enveloped her, and tears were already rising to her eyes, but suddenly she asked herself: to whom was she saying this? Where was he, and who was he now? And again everything was obscured by dry, harsh bewilderment, and again, drawing her brows together tensely, she peered toward where he was. And now, at any moment, it seemed to her, she would penetrate the mystery... But at the very moment when the incomprehensible seemed about to reveal itself to her, the loud rattle of the door-lock handle struck painfully upon her hearing. Quickly and incautiously, with a frightened expression on her face that was not concerned with Natasha, the maid Dunyasha entered the room.

“Please come to Papa, quickly,” Dunyasha said with a peculiar, animated expression. “A misfortune, about Pyotr Ilyich... a letter,” she said with a sob.

II.

Besides a general feeling of estrangement from all people, Natasha at that time experienced a particular feeling of estrangement from the members of her family. All her own people—her father, mother, Sonya—were so close to her, so familiar, so commonplace, that all their words and feelings seemed to her an affront to the world in which she had been living lately, and she was not only indifferent but looked at them with hostility. She heard Dunyasha’s words about Pyotr Ilyich, about a misfortune, but did not understand them.

“What misfortune can they have there, what misfortune could there be? Everything with them is the same old, familiar, peaceful thing,” Natasha said inwardly.

When she entered the hall, her father was coming quickly out of the countess’s room. His face was wrinkled and wet with tears. He had evidently run out of that room to give free rein to the sobs that were choking him. On seeing Natasha, he flung up his hands in despair and burst into painful, convulsive sobs that distorted his round, gentle face.

“Pe... Petya... Go, go, she... she... is calling...” And, weeping like a child, he rapidly shuffled on his weakened legs to a chair and almost fell onto it, covering his face with his hands.

Suddenly it was as though an electric current ran through Natasha’s whole being. Something struck her heart with terrible pain. She felt terrible pain; it seemed to her that something was being torn away inside her and that she was dying. But immediately after the pain she felt herself instantly freed from the prohibition on life that had lain upon her. On seeing her father and hearing her mother’s terrible, harsh cry from behind the door, she instantly forgot herself and her grief. She ran to her father, but he, feebly waving his hand, pointed toward her mother’s door. Princess Marya, pale, her lower jaw trembling, came out through the door and took Natasha by the hand, saying something to her. Natasha neither saw nor heard her. With rapid steps she went through the door, stopped for an instant as though struggling with herself, and ran to her mother.

The countess lay in an armchair, stretched out in a strange, awkward position, and beat her head against the wall. Sonya and the other girls held her by the arms.

“Natasha, Natasha!..” the countess cried. “It isn’t true, it isn’t true... He is lying... Natasha!” she cried, pushing away those around her. “All of you go away, it isn’t true! Killed!.. Ha, ha, ha!.. It isn’t true!”

Natasha put one knee on the armchair, bent over her mother, embraced her, lifted her with unexpected strength, turned her face toward herself, and pressed close to her.

Mademoiselle Georges looked sternly and gloomily over the audience and began to recite in French some verses that spoke of her criminal love for her son. At times she raised her voice, at times she whispered, solemnly lifting her head; at times she paused and rasped, rolling her eyes.

“Adorable, divine, delicious!” was heard on all sides.

Natasha looked at the stout Georges, but heard nothing, saw nothing, and understood nothing of what was taking place before her; she only felt herself once again wholly and irrevocably in that strange, mad world, so remote from her former world, in that world in which it was impossible to know what was good, what was bad, what was reasonable, and what was mad. Anatole was sitting behind her, and, feeling his nearness, she waited fearfully for something.

After the first monologue, the whole company rose and surrounded Mademoiselle Georges, expressing their delight to her.

“How good she is!” Natasha said to her father, who had risen with the others and was making his way through the crowd toward the actress.

“I do not think so, looking at you,” said Anatole, following Natasha. He said this at a moment when she alone could hear him. “You are enchanting... From the moment I saw you, I have not ceased...”

“Come, come, Natasha,” said the count, returning for his daughter. “How good she is!”

Without saying anything, Natasha went up to her father and looked at him with questioning, astonished eyes.

After several more recitations, Mademoiselle Georges left, and Countess Bezukhov asked the company to go into the ballroom.

The count wanted to leave, but Hélène begged him not to spoil her improvised ball. The Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha to waltz, and during the waltz, as he pressed her waist and hand, he told her that she was ravishing and that he loved her. During the écossaise, which she again danced with Kuragin, when they were alone, Anatole said nothing to her and merely looked at her. Natasha was in doubt as to whether she had dreamed what he had said to her during the waltz. At the end of the first figure, he pressed her hand again. Natasha raised frightened eyes to him, but there was such a self-assuredly tender expression in his affectionate gaze and smile that, looking at him, she could not say what she had meant to say to him. She lowered her eyes.

“Do not say such things to me; I am engaged and I love another,” she said quickly... She glanced at him. Anatole was neither disconcerted nor distressed by what she had said.

“Do not speak to me about that. What do I care?” he said. “I tell you that I am madly, madly in love with you. Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... We must begin.”

Animated and anxious, Natasha looked around her with wide-open, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She remembered almost nothing of what happened that evening. They danced the écossaise and the Grossvater; her father asked her to leave, and she begged to stay. Wherever she was and whoever she spoke to, she felt his gaze upon her. Later she remembered that she had asked her father’s permission to go to the dressing room to straighten her dress, that Hélène had followed her, laughing as she spoke to her about her brother’s love, and that in the small sitting room she had met Anatole again, that Hélène had disappeared somewhere, that they had been left alone, and that Anatole, taking her hand, had said in a tender voice:

“I cannot visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Never?...” And, blocking her way, he brought his face closer to hers.

His large, shining, masculine eyes were so close to her eyes that she saw nothing but those eyes.

“Natalie?!” his voice whispered questioningly, and someone was painfully squeezing her hands. “Natalie?!”

“I understand nothing; I have nothing to say,” said her gaze.

Hot lips pressed against her lips, and at that same moment she felt herself free again, and the sound of Hélène’s footsteps and rustling dress was heard in the room. Natasha looked around at Hélène, then, red and trembling, looked at him fearfully and questioningly and went toward the door.

“One word, just one, in God’s name,” Anatole was saying.

She stopped. She so needed him to say that word which would explain to her what had happened and to which she would give him an answer.

“Nathalie, one word, just one,” he kept repeating, evidently not knowing what to say, and he repeated it until Hélène came up to them.

Hélène and Natasha returned to the drawing room together. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

After returning home, Natasha did not sleep all night: she was tormented by the insoluble question of whom she loved, Anatole or Prince Andrei. She loved Prince Andrei—she clearly remembered how strongly she loved him. But she loved Anatole too; that was beyond doubt. “Otherwise, could all this have happened?” she thought. “If, after this, when saying good-bye to him, I could answer his smile with a smile, if I could allow it to come to this, it means that I loved him from the first moment. It means that he is kind, noble, and splendid, and it was impossible not to love him. What am I to do when I love him and love another?” she said to herself, finding no answers to these terrible questions.

XIV.

Morning came with its cares and bustle. Everyone got up, began moving about and talking; the dressmakers came again, Marya Dmitrievna appeared again, and they were called to tea. With her eyes wide open, as though she wished to intercept every gaze directed at her, Natasha looked uneasily at everyone and tried to seem just as she had always been.

After breakfast, Marya Dmitrievna—this was her best time—sat down in her armchair and called Natasha and the old count over to her.

“Well now, my friends, I have thought the whole matter over, and here is my advice,” she began. “Yesterday, as you know, I went to Prince Nikolai; well, and I talked to him... He took it into his head to shout. But he cannot outshout me! I told him everything!”

“But what did he say?” asked the count.

“What did he say? The madcap... He will not listen; but what is the use of talking? As it is, we have tormented the poor girl enough,” said Marya Dmitrievna. “And my advice to you is to finish your business and go home, to Otradnoe... and wait there...”

“Oh, no!” Natasha cried out.

“No, you must go,” said Marya Dmitrievna. “And wait there. If the bridegroom comes here now, there is bound to be a quarrel; but there, alone with the old man, he will discuss everything, and then he will come to you.”

Ilya Andreyevich approved of this proposal, immediately understanding all its reasonableness. If the old man softened, it would be all the better to visit him in Moscow or at Bald Hills afterward; if not, they could marry against his will only at Otradnoe.
